Question: Why are the Chinese claiming they are the oldest civilization, when they didn’t even exist when languages were developed? The Chinese lasted only 2,000 years. How did they maintain that long?
Answer: Well, America is the flagbearer of western civilization and it's all of 250 years old. And where did western civilization originate? Modern day middle-east/Mediterranean. America is an ocean away, but it spells in the Latin alphabet, and prints “in God we trust” on its currency. Clearly, western civilization is unbroken, because it can be traced from the time of the ancient sumerians, Egyptians and Persians, as recorded in the Bible. In fact, the way we tell time today is based on a recorded event in the bible: the birth of Jesus. Hence it is AD 2024 today. Anno Domini, Latin for “in the year of our lord”. But is it continuous, in the sense that today's Americans share cultural and historical commonality with others that also identify as western and those that came before them? The modern American may read Tacitus, quote Plato, and study machiavelli, but he doesn't identify as a Roman, Greek or Italian. The refrain “it's all Greek to me” is illuminating. In other words, western civilization share a loosely linked pool of knowledge, but what sets the westerner apart is still geography and DNA. After all, North Africa and the Middle East have suffered massive destruction in recent years despite being the cradle of western civilization. China is different. The fossil and DNA record clearly show modern Chinese are descended from paleolithic ancestors who settled and called it home. Elements of Neolithic culture found their way into the earliest xia and shang dynasties, including burial practices and cultural wares. Chinese writing can be traced to the oracle bones of the Shang, and character evolution remains a topic for active scholarship. There was a period of fragmentation during the long decline of the zhou in the spring-autumn and warring states, but qin unification consolidated Chinese block writing. It has remained a consistent whole for the past 2,200 years. The answer to “what it means to be Chinese” is rooted in continuity. History, culture, language, philosophy, the arts, technology, even governance and politics. Take for example the genealogy of confucius, which has been continuously maintained over 2,500 years tracing more than 80 generations, the world's longest extant record of human pedigree. There are over 2 million living descendants registered, with the estimated total well in excess of 3 million. Similarly, an educated Chinese youth today can visit the Shandong museum and read Sun Tzu's art of war off 2,200 year-old bamboo strips written during the Han dynasty. You can't do that with spelled languages. Even Shakespeare's prose is unwieldy to the point of being unreadable because a 4-century gap separates modern English from the romance of Shakespearean times. Chinese is drawn, not spelled. To be continued…

There are practically no traces of the quintessential Lee family here, other than the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, and the Lee Kuan Yew Gold Medal awarded to valedictorians in NUS and NTU. What cult? As for freedom, I have many Taiwanese friends. I have not heard them complain about a lack of freedom in Singapore, other than the colorful politics back home. In fact, one friend pointedly criticized Taiwan's lack of freedom. “In Singapore, I can ride my scooter anywhere, whereas there are scooter restrictions within Taiwan's road system.” Mostly, complaints about Singapore boil down to cost of living. Yes, food and transport is cheaper in Taiwan but wages are way higher in Singapore. That has nothing to do with “freedom”.

Question: How does Bill Chen see India?
Answer: My friend from Punjab asked for an answer years ago. I must have forgotten, because the question isn't in the list of drafts. Recently, he asked again, and I am in no position to decline. First, have I been to India? Yes, I visited Mumbai, on the invitation of a friend who spent years serving the poor. I've also been to Tamil Nadu and Kerala for business. However, I have avoided taking a closer look at India because China was the bigger draw, and there was the intuitive grasp of language and culture. It was only in the covid lull that I really took time to read up on India, especially what Indians thought of India. Unfortunately, the first 50 books (mostly economics and geopolitics) disappointed. I hope for better in the second 50 (mostly history and culture), though I have yet to start. I asked my Punjab friend for english translations of Indian classics written in the various Indian tongues. He managed to compile a list of Malayalam, urdu, Tamil, hindi, kannada and of course, Punjabi plus several other titles. It was this experience that solidified the thesis of a thousand indias in my mind, because the Indian federation is a mini UN unto itself. In fact, India may well be more culturally diverse than the 50 countries of Europe, which share only 3 alphabets: Latin, Greek and Cyrillic. Indian literature isn't one literature like the Chinese. In fact, the various traditions read like snapshots from different worlds at different times. The Jataka tales and sutras transport us to ancient India, centered around buddha's spiritual enlightenment. Even older vedas weave a rich tapestry of knowledge celebrated for their authoritative oral transmission of Hindu philosophy, rituals, mantras, meditation and worship. And yet, India is also home to the Guru Granth Sahib, the final guru of sikhism. It reads almost modern, for a religious text, because well, it only landed in the 1600s. The myths and tales in the various Indian languages read so wildly different it's hard to imagine these peoples were geographic neighbors for millennia. India reminds me of Papua New Guinea, where nearby communities are unaware of each other's presence due to the mountainous terrain, evolving distinct languages and cultures through isolation. The cause of the stable continuity is the same reason why India can support the same population as China on a third the land. One will be hard-pressed to match south Asian history with china's unenviable record of repeat invasions, civil wars and natural disasters that resulted in massive loss of life and displacement of people. In a nutshell, Indian lands were stable and rich enough for people to stay put and close ranks when there was trouble beyond. Were the communities isolated? It appears not, because this was xuanzang's travels through India 1,500 years ago. Evidently, there were established networks and knowledge of lands faraway. There remains intra-inclusivity, and inter-exclusivity in the south Asian equilibrium we call India today. The incredible separation of powers on the subcontinent isolated by the impassable himalayas meant that India has never been centrally administered, not even by the Raj or the Indian federation today. After all, hollywood can't sell its movies with a single set of subtitles in India. Neither are there universal Indian heroes, emperors/dynasties or legends. To be continued…

Question: Why did the Japanese regard the Chinese as "superior" and do Japanese in Japan still hold such beliefs? Why is China on the rise and Japan in decline and going extinct? Is Japan going extinct? Is Japan going the way of the dinosaur?

China fell behind Japan in the industrial age, but it is catching up today. It is the number one exporter of high tech goods, whereas Japan exports even less than tiny Singapore. It is a different 21st century, with heisei and reiwa unable to reverse the decline from showa Japan. Is Japan going extinct? No. But it has to tread very carefully in the reiwa era. East Asia is not quick to forget the horrors visited by imperial Japan, which is still imperial by the way, with the emperor the head of state, and vital to the people. Question: Do Chinese today believe Ancient India was inferior to Ancient China?
Answer: Let's detour to Buddhism for a bit. Buddha was born 2,500 years ago in lumbini, modern day Nepal. He died 175km away in Kushinagar, modern day uttar pradesh, India. Nalanda mahavihara was founded 1,000 years after buddha's death. It's 400km from lumbini, in modern day bihar, India. It was the greatest center for Buddhist learning in the ancient world, and the source of the scriptures sought by the tang dynasty monk xuanzang, forever immortalized in the Chinese epic journey to the west. That was AD 629-645. India was the heartbeat of Buddhism, the fountain of Buddhist teaching. Modern Buddhists, however, have to rely on Xuanzang's translations to back out lost sanskrit texts. The oldest and most complete Buddhist scriptures and records are no longer found in India. They reside in monasteries found in Sri Lanka, Tibet, Thailand and China. Siddhartha's enlightenment was extinguished in India. And that is the problem with studying ancient India, because there are significant gaps in the historical record. Yes, Nalanda definitely existed, and it was one of the greatest universities of its era. But what was taught? How was it funded? How was it administered? What was the lineage of the masters who led it? We don't know, beyond the scraps inferred from myriad sources. Whereas the Chinese kept such detailed dynastic records that when a new tomb is discovered, the owner of the tomb can often be traced in the written records. Another clear example is the genealogy record of confucius, now into the 83rd generation spanning more than 2,500 years. It is the longest extant record of pedigree in human history. As my Punjab friend likes to say, Indian history is at best, patchy beyond the vedas. No other people or civilization can compare with the voluminous detail found in the Chinese written record. In other words, the Chinese have maintained the most comprehensive and unbroken database of recorded human experience over the past 3,500 years. The basis for comparison does not exist, and “inferior” is a poor choice of words. Note: Shaolin was founded around AD 500, the same time as Nalanda. It is still continuing the lineage of Damo at Songshan today.

Question: In hindsight and as a Singaporean do you feel as though opening Singapore's first casino in Singapore was a blessing or a mistake? Did it create social problems? If so, did the benefits outweigh the social problems they have caused?
Answer: Well, to be accurate, Singapore granted two casino licenses, one to Las Vegas Sands and the other to Genting. People tend to remember only marina bay sands, because the other is tucked away on sentosa. The last time I was at the latter, I was surprised by the number of Malaysia registered vehicles at the carpark. There were even a few Thai plates. I was there for a show at the attached theater. It is an INTEGRATED resort, after all. Now, why were sands and Genting chosen? To my mind, they had the connections to bring in the hottest acts from both east and west, and firmly establish Singapore on the international tour circuit. Not that casino operations haven't been profitable here. Far from it. But the predatory practices common elsewhere are largely absent in Singapore. Singapore does not have an organized crime presence, while moneylending is a licensed and heavily regulated industry. Beyond the daily entrance levy chargeable for Singapore residents, there is an additional, more effective safeguard against financial ruin due to problem gambling—the HDB flat, which is linked to the retirement account. Many people do not know that the HDB unit is excluded from the flat owner's list of assets in the event of a personal bankruptcy. Creditors cannot make a claim on a HDB property, if at least one owner is a Singapore citizen. Since the majority stay in public housing, schemes to seize property to repay gambling debts are dead in the water. Among my parents’ crowd, that is older, social gamblers, they prefer the more affordable cruise to nowhere option, where the casino rooms open once the ship reaches international waters. I've heard of a few problem cases, but the bad debts are exclusively among friends, because the casino management will not extend credit, just like in the IRs. Overall, the licensed money lenders have not fueled gambling addiction. The introduction of the IRs have not fostered an increase in crime, or gambling related issues, either (problem gambling has remained stable at 1% of the population). The junkets are also among the cleanest in the Asia pacific, ahead of Australia, and Macau. On balance, I'd say sands and Genting are seen as healthy (if pricy) family entertainment centers rather than sleazy, crime infested addiction dens.

Question: Is there any other writing system that works like Chinese? It allows speakers of unrelated languages or distantly related languages to understand each other when writing, and modern people to understand 2000-3000 year old texts.
Answer: In terms of being a language family that enjoys unbroken continuity and in active use today? No. Yes, there are a number of ancient, pre-AD languages in use today. But they all suffer lock-in, because the written form, to a fault, spell sounds (or syllables) from a set of letters, also known as an alphabet. What is lock-in? The exclusive set of sounds and unique combinations that make up the spoken or oral language. For example, French and English are both spelled with latin letters, but knowledge of English does not allow one to read French, and vice versa, because the sound combinations are exclusive, with the exception of loan words. Written Chinese isn’t spelled. It is drawn. Chinese block writing obeys a simple rule. One block, one character, one sound (syllable). Each character represents a word with meaning. Each Chinese dialect overlays a separate, independent sound layer on the same set of characters, which allows a single script to be used across all dialects. How block writing unlocks the past is the unbroken logical foundations constantly being refined and updated with the times, allowing modern characters to share sufficient commonality with more ancient scripts to be decoded. More importantly, the ideas and databank from which they are drawn have been continuously maintained and expanded for millennium, allowing modern Chinese readers to draw from the same pool of knowledge.

Question: Why do some Chinese companies such as Huawei, BYD, and Luckin Coffee grow much faster than U.S. companies in the same sector?

Herein lies the rub. Public companies have to double down on growth at all cost, otherwise they start falling by the wayside, stock price wise. A diligent MBA will be able to crunch the numbers and estimate the raw profit from every cuppa Starbucks sells. That’s margin, and the starting point for any upstart aiming for a seat at the table, assuming one has a competitive product to sell. Upstarts trade margin for market share, simple as that. Yes, it’s capital intensive, but increasingly, capital is turning its head from export-driven companies. Rather, domestic capital is focused on growing local champions capable of challenging foreign big boys. Best thing is, upstarts don’t have the pressure of shareholder dividends and quarterlys. Luckin is one such beneficiary, because its strategy of fishing where Starbucks isn’t casting nets has drawn rich dividends. Luckin’s investment in lower-tier city outlets offering the “Starbucks experience at Luckin prices” has been a roaring success. Yes, margin is traded for market share, but brand recognition is worth far, far more. Barring a coffee catastrophe, today’s kids will be drinking Luckin tomorrow, and Starbucks better be prepared for a drawn-out multidimensional war, be it price, media saturation, outlet density or product quality/differentiation. It may sound frivolous, but first world business models have first world economics baked in. Factor in the strong dollar/Euro and in earlier years the strong Won/Yen, and profit repatriation limit the cost/clientele baseline. For example, Apple iPhones used to cost more in China than in Japan, which enjoyed some of the lowest prices in Asia. First world businesses focus primarily on the prosperous middle class, leaving 800–1b consumers underserved. This is where local competition come in, because they can operate on mainland cost and profit structures internally while trimming the frills to deliver products that may be compromised but competitive externally, especially if they identify and focus on specific demographics/geographies. In that fiery cauldron, thousands of companies compete to survive, with the winners emerging as domestic champions, fit as hell and armed with a hyper-competitive business model that’s infinitely adapatable, and incredibly nimble. That’s what it takes to climb to the top in China, because any fat in a mainland business is honey-to-badgers for the hungry competition. Witness Haidilao’s rise from tiny restaurant started with 8,000 yuan in 1994 to international hotpot chain today, renowned for its use of AI-driven automation and operations. Foreign companies can’t keep up, mostly, because it is too painful to cannibalize existing margin for a future that’s still many years away. That’s the story of ICE cars, with the competiton caught pants down, because the Chinese announced the future has arrived and is here to stay. Students of history will draw parallels with Mao’s famous strategy of 农村包围城市 proposed in 1928 that drew on the principle 星星之火，可以燎原. Translated, start small, away from the attention of the competition you cannot yet beat. And that’s what the Chinese did. The first EVs in China didn’t look like this: Instead they looked like this: Enabled by this humble little bugger being churned out by the million in the smartphone revolution: By the decade of the 2010s, lithium-based battery chemistry had sufficient energy density and stability for use in high current draw applications. Best of all, the R&D was paid by the humongous profit generated from smartphone sales, and EVs hopped on as a freeloader. What the Chinese did different was to focus on affordability and usability. The earliest EV products did not require specialized charging networks. Rather, they were sold as appliances (electric skate scooters etc) and tools (3-wheel farming tractors). But making these at scale allowed the supply chain upstream to iterate constant improvement in batteries, motors, sensors, suspension and controls. It is this core competency that companies like BYD tapped into, with the government roped in to build the nationwide charging grid as the EV population expanded. This synergy of bottom-up organic and top-down directed growth is explosive, and possibly unique today. To be continued…

Question: How long can China maintain its current rate of manufacturing jobs?

There will be fewer Chinese workers going forward, but we are talking about the world’s largest labor pool that’s 5x the size of America, the world’s 3rd largest. The Chinese labor pool is equal to 1 India + 2 America, approximately. Wages will rise, but so will output, with fewer workers employed. That’s inevitable, because the replacement labor is way better qualified than those retiring.

Question: Is the Chinese economy essentially a Ponzi Scheme, where the CCP is actually borrowing from its own citizens to keep things afloat day-to-day? How long can this go on for, before the whole thing crashes?
Answer: Recently, I sat in on a session introducing several trading instruments, and it included an acronym making the rounds recently, the CLO, or the Collateralized Loan Obligation. Now, in finance, anything that ends with the term “Obligation” is more likely than not, a derivative. That is, the product’s value isn’t intrinsic, but derived from underlying assets. The CLO is a close cousin of the notorious CDO, or Collateralized Debt Obligation, which burned down both Bear Stearns and Lehman. Beyond its size (>$1 trillion value-at-risk), there was a particular nugget that caught my attention: the annual return for the CLO investor post-GFC averaged 15%, and could exceed 30% depending on tranche. In other words, in a typical 12-year life of a CLO, the investor can expect between 180–360% profit on the sum invested. Now, companies obviously don’t borrow at 15–30% rates. Even credit card overdrafts which are open-ended (and hence compounded) have an APR in the 20+% range. How does the CLO vehicle generate high returns? And why is the CLO absent beyond the first world? Answer the above and they will disprove the thesis posed. Now, China’s capital markets are not correlated with the economy. The stock market has repeatedly crashed this century, while GDP grew merrily, double digits at times. China is 35% of global manufacturing currently, and will exceed 50% by 2040. In the last two years, the economy has grown by >5% per annum while experiencing a variety of market-disrupting forces, including a collapse in asset prices. In other words, strong growth when a balance sheet recession is more reasonable. Why? A ponzi is primarily a redistribution scam, using new deposits to fund withdrawals. Typically, there is no economic benefit created, and the primary beneficiary is the scam operator. The Chinese economy is delivering real, measurable, quality of life improvement, doing so even through covid. From healthcare, to education, from housing, to connectivity. Inflation that has burned through all first world economies has largely skipped the mainland. This can be verified by the lopsided change in the nominal GDP/GDP (PPP) ratio since 2019. Chinese GDP growth delivers real progress to the life of the average Chinese citizen, rural or urban. You can’t say the same for the G7/G20. How does the CLO vehicle generate high returns? For the investor, the CLO is a LEVERAGED product, typically 10x or more. The thoughtful question to ask is, who provides the leverage? Which also answers the second question, about the absence of the CLO beyond the first world. The societies playing the numbers game to drive the wealth effect are mostly first world. Otherwise, we won’t have stock market highs in the midst of a recession, or economic growth while parents struggle to feed their children, and retirees priced out of winter heating. In the ultimate analysis, it is outcomes delivered and lived by citizens that is the true barometer of economic progress and benefit. Inhabitants of a distorted ponzi reality won’t enjoy year-on-year progress beyond the wealth effect. Then again, most will only enjoy the performance as the audience, and not the beneficiary.

Question: What do you think of the theories of Confucius from China?
Answer: The central theme of Confucius’ teaching revolve around the character 仁: It is formed from two radicals, which literally means “two persons” or 人与人. 仁 is translated as compassion, benevolence or being humane. In essence, Confucius taught his disciples about human relationships. He laid out rules for various relationships found in human society, such as parent-child, between siblings, uncle-cousin, elder-youngster, teacher-student, leader-follower and so on. In other words, Confucius promulgated rules to cultivate the various forms of relationship in society, with the ultimate aim being harmony at all levels of society. Perhaps this is why people often have the mistaken impression that Confucianism makes for dry and dreary reading. But was Confucius focused exclusively on process? No. He was all about outcomes. For example, he was known to give different advice to various disciples, even lying on occasion. He understood that individuals had different nature, especially character strengths and weaknesses and the same message can be interpreted different. Confucius had gone beyond process. He was a master focused on outcomes, which was the expression of the student’s greatest potential. That’s why I consider Deng a Confucian at heart, because he exhorted the Chinese nation to “摸石头过河” and “抓到老鼠就是好猫”. Outrageous perhaps, but the same laser focus on outcome. So what is my takeaway from Confucianism? Human society is two or more persons. And harmony in society can only be achieved with compassion and benevolence. Rules and boundaries are there to help the average individual stay on the straight and narrow. But human nature trumps all rules. In the final analysis, Confucius may have been a Taoist at heart. 点到为止。 YMMV. 子曰：不患人之不己知，患不知人也。

Question: China built 10 missile cruisers in 48 months, packing 1,120 missiles.It's true? Why can't the US do the same? Doesn't the US have a larger defense budget?
Answer: If this is in reference to the Type 055 program, it’s 8 in 8 years (2014–2022), from hull-laying to commission. That’s probably unmatched delivery schedule, for a brand new >10,000 tonne warship class. The impressive aspect of this program is the abrupt announcement of the program’s existence and the decision to serially produce an initial batch of 8 ships. Usually, yards take their time to construct and test the lead ship of a new class, which serve as a systems demonstrator. Evidently, the engineers must have tested the individual subsystems to death to confidently build the ships in parallel. By all indications, Nanchang, the lead ship, has fulfilled its operating envelop. There are plans in place for another batch of 8. The American Arleigh-Burke, in its third iteration from 1980s roots, is also being laid and commissioned at a rate 1 per year. It is the only American destroyer in production currently, and displaces ~9,000 tonnes. The difference between the Americans and Chinese is the latter operating more than one Destroyer class. The Type 052D is a 7,500 tonne-class warship announced in 2012. Construction probably begun in 2010. Between 2010–2022, 25 ships have been laid and commissioned, for a rate of ~2 per year. In other words, China’s demonstrated destroyer output in the past decade and a half is at least 3 per year. Going forward, it is estimated that the Type 052DL program will deliver 3–4 ships per year. If the Type 055 program is expanded, that’s 4–5 destroyers a year in the coming decade. America has had immense difficulty delivering clean-sheet designs this century. Even the Constellation class, which is developed off a licensed and proven FREMM design from the 2000s has run into construction snags. The problem? Backlog and lack of skilled workers. Fundamentally, American shipbuilding is in a horrible state of neglect, with heavy shipbuilding a dead end commercially. Only military shipyards remain viable, and there is a general lack of skilled workers in the industry. Boomer retirement is eroding institutional memory, while union protectionism add to self-renewal woes. China has over 500,000 workers in the shipbuilding industry, which produced >50% of the global merchant tonnage delivered last year. There are at least 30–40 dry docks that can accommodate >100,000-tonne ships. Chinese shipyards are now capable of building the most challenging designs, such as ice-breakers, LNG carriers and ocean liners, using precision-controlled hull block modular construction techniques that significantly reduce build times and defects. American shipbuilding suffer from a deficit in scale, and increasingly, skill and technology.

And yet the Russian economy grew strongly last year, despite a tepid international environment. The Russians are a country that produce extraordinary chess champions, mathematicians, physicists, economists, politicians. The harsh winters have made the Russians a tough and resilient people who thrive in hardship. Russia is now facing an existential threat from the West, and the challenge being met by a people who have given Putin the mandate to pivot East. Russia IS Asian and it has a big role to play as a major pole in the emerging multi-polar world order. There are things China can do that Russia can’t. Similarly, Russia wields influence and has capabilities China doesn’t. A brave new world can emerge ahead of schedule if both cooperate. China’s primary task remains domestic renovation to catch up with the first world. Russia too. To say Russia is utterly reliant on China misses the forest for the trees. I prefer “the sum is greater than the whole”. Russia isn’t trying to change China, and vice versa. There is massive benefit in cooperation and exchange, and long may it continue as the two giants of Eurasia remake the world.

This is a win-win in most cases, lucrative and steady revenue stream for the contractor, and optimized uptime for the factory. And according to the grapevine, this has been ongoing for several years, albeit informally in a go slow manner involving key parts and chemicals, particularly targeting SMIC. Evidently, SMIC managed to bash its way through the prejudice, though I am not privy to the details except its volume and balance sheet remain healthy. To openly suggest that contracts with the Chinese NEED NOT BE HONORED is a whole new level of hurt, and opens the door to retaliation and honestly, chaos. Any company or group of companies trying that can permanently kiss the Chinese market goodbye, because evil thought must be nipped at the bud lest the entire house burns down. The risk to ASML as an upstream toolmaker is two-fold. Within the mainland, prudent risk management will force the Chinese to develop indigenous alternatives that may adopt the Indian interpretation of pharmaceutical IP (i.e. patent applications must be sufficiently novel or groundbreaking to qualify for issuance) or consider them non-commercial tools. As long as alternatives exist, ASML and other toolmakers will not commit hara-kiri to pursue obscene acts of prejudice. The other problem is ex-China, overcapacity develops as China ramps up production. Even legacy or bread-and-butter chips from say TI or any number of established names will come under assault as the Chinese form beachheads to challenge strangleholds. This will profoundly reshape the volume and composition of chips made ex-China. Both developments in tandem will force toolmakers and other upstream suppliers to pull out all tricks in order to retain the one market that has stable and strong growth over a long horizon. Eventually, China will make the best chips at every price point. The question is, are you ready to accept such a projection? I expect ASML to merge back with Phillips eventually, unless there is a radical rethink.

Question: Taiwan’s air defense density is so high, how can mainland China break through?

There were Aegis systems on USN ships, land-based THAAD and Patriot batteries, airborn fighters guided by awacs and Israel’s own Iron Dome forming a multi-layered defense system with over 1,500km of strategic depth. More than $1b in munitions was expended to counter the Iranian assault, which totaled a measly ~200 drones and cruise/hypersonic missiles. That’s a far more comprehensive and extravagant air defense than Taiwan can possibly field, if only because the mainland is less than 200km from Taiwan’s coast and the island a mere 400 km long and 150 km across with no strategic depth to speak of. And yet, Iranian hypersonic missiles got through and hit one of the most well-protected and sensitive airbases in the Negev housing the F-35, to prove a point. These weren’t even the most advanced and potent missiles in the Iranian arsenal. Now, is anyone willing to bet the Chinese don’t have better missiles in both quality and quantity? You only need to destroy air defenses once, and China has tactical rocket artillery that can rain fire from the sky 24.7 to mop up or suppress the enemy. And we have not included the air force and navy, which have bombs and missiles aplenty. Good luck.

Question: The Chinese Diaspora is large and economically free. What changes would the CCP have to make to attract them home? Are there enough of them to overcome the birth rate crash?

Recently, my friend said Shanghai is trialing a bubble tea outlet with a single employee, whose job is to troubleshoot the various robots/thingmajigs running the place. Everything is automated. In rural China, even the farming equipment are being electrified, and traditionally labor-intensive tasks such as the spraying of fertilizer and herbicide sub-contracted to drone operators. It is possible for a single farmer to farm his property using pooled assets and automation. This may sound offensive to some but China has an overhang of poorly educated folk, mostly the generations born before the 90s. China has overachieved, from a population base that is more poorly educated on average than India. And China can shed 300m jobs (that’s 1 India+2 Americas) before reaching parity in labor pool size with India. 300,000,000 is a LOT of jobs.

Question: Is Comac hiding its technological progress and misleading Biden by showing a long time horizon to avoid a trade war?
Answer: No. Airliners is a special business, even within aviation. Why? They carry passengers in the tens to hundreds. That is why there is extraordinary scrutiny on the entire system, down to the stewardess serving cup noodles on budget flights. Yes, she has to obtain a type certification, just like the pilots, and it is specific to the airliner model. The same goes for the maintenance crew—everyone is trained, tested and certified, with the cycle repeated to maintain currency. This extraordinary level of training and oversight is what makes flying far safer than driving. Every physical part of an airliner is tested to death, especially the engines. Even the number of coats of paint is a controlled spec, not only because paint add weight to the airframe, but the thickness can alter the operation of moving parts, especially the control surfaces. Comac has recently introduced its first narrowbody six-across C919. It is at the most painful stage currently, ironing out teething issues for the early jets, while ramping up production to fulfill the burgeoning order book. It will have to document every spec, down to the training requirements for technicians and crew, and make the material broadly available to all customers and regulators. It will have to publish procedures for the safe operation and maintenance of the aircraft, and establish the technical limits of the airframe and moving parts. All these take time, especially if one starts from a clean sheet, and the entire process is regulated by authorities, who will have to sign off on the type certification. It is a rigorous process that takes lots of time.

Question: Japan and the Netherlands agreed with the U.S. to restrict exports of advanced chip-manufacturing equipment to China. How will it hurt China's chip industry?
Answer: What’s the feedback loop here? Politically, US leaders don’t want China anywhere near sub-10nm production, and Chinese volume production of any chip like that will be met with further sanction expansion. SMIC has managed to produce 5nm gen 2 equivalent chips using DUV, which has not been used for volume production under 10nm. But that’s besides the point. ASML is a tool manufacturer. Its revenue is dependent on capacity expansion, i.e. new chip production lines. Guess where the capacity expansion is happening? China is ASML’s largest customer, especially for mature node technologies, and there is a gold rush going on, because the capacity expansion in China was not part of the business forecast, not even by the Chinese themselves. China’s chip expansion in recent years wasn’t part of the current 5-year plan. The Huawei sanctions and abuse of IP rights forced the Chinese hand, and they are pursuing an at-all-cost strategy of chip independence across the spectrum. Now, fabs are probably the most expensive factories in history. Each can cost 10 or 11 figures to build. Dollars, not yuan. Local governments have to get in on the act, providing ample land, infrastructure, and massive amounts of clean water and electricity. Knowing the glut of new Chinese chip supply that is coming online every year, ex-China competitors are reluctant to invest in new capacity, because they are losing their best customer. China, the largest chip consumer globally, is shedding chip import at an astonishing rate. Back to ASML and other tool/material suppliers. They are seeing strong demand vis-a-vis China, and slowing demand ex-China for volume products. China is already >30% of global capacity in terms of wafer production. It will hit 40% in a few years. Within the decade, half of all chips will be made in China, and China will morph into a net chip exporter in both volume and value. There will be serious overcapacity ex-China, and the enablers—the toolmakers and specialty raw material suppliers will come under immense Chinese competition that is being incubated today, cocooned by a national strategy of prudent risk management. How will ASML et al. choose? Reject the customer keeping the numbers afloat and it may delay the Chinese for a few years, but also lose access to where the action is going forward. China is fundamentally reshaping the global chip business. My friend predicts prices will bite hard in the coming chip winter ex-China, enough to shrink aggregate capacity significantly. I find it highly plausible.

Question: Big scandals and corruption is bleeding many developing economies. What can we learn from China or other successful nations?
Answer: Many people do not know that the Tiananmen protests of 1989 wasn’t about democracy or freedom. The main demand was for the government to extinguish corruption and return to socialist days of the iron rice bowl. People wanted the old system back, one without the corrosive influence of money. China has had massive corruption problems since the very beginning of reform and opening up, and that’s the last 4 decades since the 1980s. The situation only turned in the 2010s, when Xi Jinping came to power, and corruption is markedly reduced today. Unfortunately, the asset expansion in the Chinese economy means even village chiefs can accumulate billion-yuan ill-gotten gains, and corruption scandals still make dramatic news today. In other words, fewer but no less spectacular, for different reasons. I will not furnish details except to make a poignant observation. China grew explosively during the years when it was most corrupt (>10%), and the Xi administration is presiding over the slowest growing (5–7%) but cleanest China since Deng changed course. Let me repeat. China grew explosively during the years when it was most corrupt (>10%), and the Xi administration is presiding over the slowest growing (5–7%) but cleanest China since Deng changed course. Which begs the question: is corruption good? Or is there something unique about Chinese corruption? But first, what is corruption? The dictionary defines it as “dishonest or illegal behavior involving a person in a position of power”. Keep that in mind, as we take a short spin of China during the teething Deng years. China was 20% urbanized in 1980. The slogans of the time were 想致富先修路，摸石头过河，不管黑猫白猫 捉到老鼠就是好猫。 China had very little money supply, because it was a command economy. It was still primarily agrarian, having suffered embargo and isolation by both superpowers—the US and the USSR for decades. In fact, the Cultural Revolution was Mao’s effort to deurbanize, because industrialization and growth could not be sustained with the withdrawal of Soviet support. More importantly, China was still poorly connected, and rural China functioned as independent and largely isolated pods of economic activity. The annals of Chinese crime is replete with serial offenders who went on years-long crime sprees, enabled by the rise of the money economy. The most heinous examples include hundreds of gang rapes and a string of home invasions that massacred entire families perpetuated by well-organized gangs who took advantage of the connectivity gaps in rural China. Now, why did I choose to highlight 3 slogans in a discussion of corruption, namely “connect communities”, “make it up as you go along” and “the end justifies the means”? What I want to emphasize is the abrupt appearance of money as THE medium of exchange as well as development of Special Economic Zones and mass industrialization introduced universal chaos into an agrarian command economy. Depending on how one judged the era, there were either no rules or rules that changed so fast it was impossible to keep up. Shenzhen (or Bao An, the old name) for example went from a sleepy town of 30,000 to 17m megacity in 40 years, attracting immigrants from all over China who caught the money and opportunity fever. In the earliest days, officials were told to practice market capitalism in the SEZs, but given little to no resources. It was just lines on a map where “different rules apply” and a promise that taxes raised in the SEZ could be retained for development. What happens when an 80% rural country industrialize? Jobs begin to appear, driving the rural-urban migration. And jobs are paid in wages. Money China didn’t have. How did those in charge of the SEZs solve the problem? The ones that succeeded traded rights to fill the coffers and drive development, especially the all-important jobs creation. to be continued…

Question: Why does China make so many fake versions of other countries’ products?
Answer: Let’s talk 2020s America and two American companies, a tiny one, and one of the world’s largest. Peak Design congratulates Amazon for copying its signature sling bag so well The differences between the two bags are bigger than the price By Ian Carlos Campbell Mar 4, 2021, 6:55 AM GMT+8 Peak Design, a maker of fine bags and accessories, has a problem: Amazon appears to have copied its popular bag, the $99.95 Everyday Sling, with its own $32.99 Amazon Basics Camera Bag. It was even called Everyday Sling until Peak Design’s video. Rather than do anything drastic, yet, Peak Design decided to make a video about what customers “gain” by purchasing Amazon’s version. The video presents Peak’s case clearly: the bags are similarly shaped, with pockets, labels, and straps in the exact same places. As someone unfamiliar with Peak Design’s bags, if I wasn’t paying attention or didn’t read “Peak Design” on the label, I’d probably mix them up. The Amazon Basics Everyday Sling on the left and Peak Design’s Everyday Sling on the right. Image: Peak Design Peak presents all of this humorously, but the evidence is surprisingly blatant, which makes Amazon’s apparent decision to change its Amazon Basics version from “Everyday Sling” to “Amazon Basics Camera Bag” all the more suspicious. There’s even evidence: “Everyday Sling” is still in the URL for the “Camera Bag.” Peak Design isn’t the first smaller company to try to stand up to Amazon. When Allbirds discovered Amazon was selling what looked like a pretty obvious Allbirds clone, the company’s CEO wrote a Medium post criticizing Amazon, even though he claimed he was “flattered” by the similarities between the shoes. Amazon’s copying hasn’t stopped there. The company’s also been accused of cloning car trunk organizers and seat cushions. Amazon and Allbirds’ shoes compared. Image: Amazon and Image: Allbirds The whole trend has only served to draw attention to a potential antitrust issue that’s long concerned the company’s critics, as well as lawmakers and regulators. The basic problem: Amazon owns and operates its e-commerce platform and also runs an ever-growing list of in-house brands that compete against Amazon’s own third-party Marketplace sellers on that same platform. Undercutting the competition is as simple, in theory, as seeing what’s selling well, creating a similar, cheaper product, and then suggesting it to Amazon shoppers. In fact, that very situation is at the heart of a European Union investigation into the company’s operations, which resulted in the European Commission accusing Amazon of “systematically” using seller data to unfairly compete against its own merchants in France and Germany last November. Amazon says it has a policy in place to prevent third-party seller data from being used for products, but reporting from The Wall Street Journal suggests it’s still happened. As Vice notes, even former CEO Jeff Bezos was unable to confirm if the policy had been broken during the House Judiciary Committee’s investigation into Amazon’s monopoly status. In Peak Design’s case, the company said in a statement to The Verge it believes Amazon has actually infringed on its intellectual property, but it chose to make the video to highlight the differences between the products and has no plans to take legal action now. Reviews are currently disabled on Amazon’s bag because the company noticed “unusual reviewing activity.” Looking at some of the newest reviews, several of the lowest ratings have been left by customers directly referencing Peak Design’s video. Taken with Amazon’s decision to change the product’s name, it seems like Peak Design has struck a chord. The Verge contacted Amazon about Peak Design’s claim and we will update if we receive a response. Yes, Amazon COPIES/RIPS OFF designs, blatantly. Why? There is margin to be made. Plenty of margin. The cost to manufacture a design is a mere fraction of the sticker price, and profit in capitalism attracts like no other perfume. Here’s an unwelcome fact. Everyone copies. If company “A” is well resourced and hires from Harvard Business School and Yale Law (and consults with McKinsey), they call it “market research” and do just enough to avoid being sued, like Amazon. If company “B” isn’t, they are named and shamed and sued till the pants drop, or sold in the black market as illegal counterfeits. Everyone copies. Including Apple. And Google. And Microsoft. And Nvidia. And Intel. Just check court records of the S&P 500. Thousands upon thousands of cases. Annually, they spend billions defending themselves or suing others for IP infringement, and all of them have lost cases and ordered to pay restitution. It’s naked capitalism and happens everywhere. The bigger the nation, the more examples one finds.

Question: After de-coupling supply chains from China, how can non-Chinese companies and countries build supply chain cost structures which are competitive against the Chinese supply chains?
Answer: Take chips and airliners, which China has had to import. China spent more on chips than oil until recently, buying hundreds of billions dollars worth every year. Why? It made few chips, especially the higher-end ones. Chips wasn’t a priority in the current 2021–2025 five year plan, because the Chinese had more pressing concerns lower down the value chain. But Huawei changed everything. China now has 30% of global chip production capacity, and will exceed 40% in a few years. There is a legitimate case for overcapacity and subsidy, on a free market basis. Unfortunately, trade flow is being reshaped by politics, rather than economics, and that is why Janet glaringly omitted CHIPS from her Beijing spiel. To emphasize, the overcapacity in chips is solely driven by America throwing its weight around to unfairly contain Chinese development in high technology, forcing the Chinese to throw restraint (and the rule book) out the window. For airliners, China didn’t make any, until recently. Comac currently has 2 models in service, the ARJ21 and the C919. In a few years, production of the C919 will be ramped up to over 200 per year, along with the introduction of the CJ-1000 engine option next to the Leap 1. The backlog of orders, currently >1,500, will take a decade to clear. The first widebodies, the C929 and C939 (the A330 and A350 equivalent) will also make commercial debut in the 2030s, along with Chinese engine options. All these form part of a broad spectrum assault up the value chain, allowing China to go from today’s 35% of global manufacturing to >50% before 2040 arrives. There will be two classes of goods in the near future: China-made or foreign made. By then, China will have an essentially complete indigenous supply chain built on IP it controls. Other than select niches such as specialty pharmaceuticals, software and machine tools, the Chinese will have competent or even superior alternatives to everything the rest of the world manufactures, from green energy to AI. The exclusivity of western high walls and deep moats will increasingly be found in the recesses of history. On to the consumer. An often underexplored angle is the end-to-end shopping experience. In today’s world, it’s the online stream that drives sales. Finding a product, choosing among options, payment and finally delivery. Today, I can order a $5 item from China, and select the 5-day guaranteed doorstep delivery for another $1.50. Amazon can’t do that. Rakuten can’t do that. Temu and Shein are absolutely smashing markets worldwide, because they are offering end-to-end apparel shopping experiences that no one else is delivering today. What’s their secret sauce? Affordable quality at the forefront of trendiness, fulfilled in a jiffy. It isn’t just cost structure, to step up to bat with the Chinese. The entire service platform including the underlying logistics is just as critical. The competition hasn’t emerged yet, but I welcome being proven wrong. Why have I expended so many words without seeming to answer the question directly? I have come around to the conclusion that cost structure is the wrong question to ask, because friend-shoring is being shaped through politics, rather than economics. The bigger change is the 1–2 trillion dollars of revenue that foreign firms generate in China, the largest single market in the world. That is why Janet and others have drawn attention to China’s “excessive household savings” and “low consumption”, calling on the government to boost demand. Foreign firms are seeing alarming shifts in Chinese demand patterns, from Tesla to Apple to Starbucks to Boeing. Will French bags, Swiss watches, German cars, Italian fashion be next? This is irreversible, as Chinese competition improve by the day, attracted by the high margin, glitzy models of western capitalism. This is the true galactic war being fought, on the mainland market, and not the friend-shoring distraction. The Chinese brands that emerge from this brutal experience will be globally competitive. Even runner-ups will be able to find niches elsewhere, such as Transsion in Africa. In other words, forget friend-shoring and competitive cost structures. Any firm that doesn’t have a place in the world’s biggest, most dynamic and competitive single market isn’t globally competitive, and will have to rely on political protection to survive. I’d like to end with a short discussion on the scale of the Chinese challenge. The strength of the Chinese come from their extraordinary ability to organize and cooperate on multiple scales, including pie-in-the-sky multi-generational goals without set horizons. The five-year plans are a good example, a top-down-bottom-up meeting of minds to drive national progress. For example, a bottom-up request to increase rural income requires top-down connectivity and power, from roads/public transport, to electric and telecoms grids, so that farmers gain market access, and talent and investment can pour in for job creation. This all-of-nation cooperation between public and private is rare, with the closest being Taiwan when the KMT was in charge. Japan and Korea both suffer from opposing clan interests, and as Japan discovered for the past 2-3 decades, competitive advantages can be rug-pulled by Uncle Sam on whim. As a national system, I believe modern day China is peerless in terms of the depth and cohesiveness of broad-spectrum cooperation. Ten, twenty years ago, Toyota kept an eye out for what Honda and Nissan were doing, followed by Hyundai and Kia, with a secondary interest in the Germans. Toyota stayed the number 1 carmaker globally wholly on merit, because it has core competencies. Fast forward to the present and Toyota is staring goggle-eyed at the millions of BEVs being churned out by the Chinese, when its own BEV presence and selection is minimal. Even Huawei and Xiaomi are churning out cars today with smart self-driving features. The cabin of a $5,000 BEV is competitive in quality, design, and features for Japanese sedans that cost multiples more. BYD is replacing shocks/springs/struts with linear motors for suspension, and it is far superior to the best the market has to offer today. BYD, one company, hires more R&D staff than foreign automakers combined. It is a different scale of challenge when BYD can add hundreds of thousands in production capacity within 12–18 months at a single site through local government support in factory building, provision of utilities, upgrading of connectivity, the hiring of staff, and approval of permits. The speed and efficiency takes the breath away. Better yet, the modern Chinese factory enjoys a high degree of automation, and production along with QC can be rapidly scaled up at other sites. One will have to copy the Chinese to keep up with the Chinese, without the advantage of market scale, and the efficiencies enabled by the public-private cooperation model. Why? The Chinese are setting the pace in Industry 5.0.

Question: Is China winning the battle of economy and technology over the U.S.?
Answer: Well, China is approaching 35% of global manufacturing capacity. It is absolutely dominant in all classes of goods in the mid- and low-end, from household wares to shoes and clothes. BYD now has world class chassis, motors, batteries, suspension, lidar/sensors, autonomous driving algorithms, and a rapidly maturing design language, both exterior and cabin. They have a full spectrum of models across the price range, and next-gen manufacturing capacity to meet exploding demand. Why? They spent the last 3 decades accumulating knowhow, and improved their wares stepwise, until they arrived as world beaters. The Germans are terrified. The Japanese are terrified. Americans will be forced to buy overpriced first world products, and this may very well contribute to a spiraling of inflation. These inefficiencies will add up, and cause American productivity to lag, as the rest of the world set free from first world tech dominance play rapid catchup, especially in the green energy, telecoms and AI segments. America no longer has the requisite environment to foster competition, other than several choice segments. The Chinese model is to fail small, and fail often, and nowhere is it more dramatic than EVs, with more than 100 domestic Chinese brands competing in the segment today. There is really only Tesla stateside, and it is facing market rejection and pushback due to a variety of factors, but especially the end of tax credits and skyrocketing cost-of-living. The compression of profit margin will force American industry to cut corners, such as reducing institutional memory, and shrinking R&D and QC budgets. We will see more Boeings and 3M down the road, all thanks to next-level profligate spending kicked off by covid. American monopolies are also being challenged, especially high-moat, high margin targets such as Apple. If anybody can do it, it is the Chinese, who are an industrious and talented people.

Yes, there are some hacks involved, but the iOS solution used to be much cleaner and reliable, because it was available as an official app on the store. Whatsapp on Android, to put it mildly, behaves funny, particularly notifications. It also varied from brand to brand. Note the above describes the mainland experience, not HK/Taiwan/Macau/rotw. Now, it is no longer available on iOS, which is notorious for being strict with sideloading. That further decreases the appeal of iphone on the mainland, because the functionality goes down.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: What reforms does India need to become a world factory like China did? How will Indians solve the problems of infrastructure, labor skills, tax incentives, corruption with a deeply divided political system that cannot find common ground in policy?
Answer: India’s problems are legion. I will just touch on one. India, by and large, remains a walled garden. And walled gardens are not too different from isolated islands. Yes, the diversity will be unique, but islands turn into time capsules, as a result of being isolated from developments elsewhere. That’s India’s economy today, which will lag behind because foreign competition are unable to compete on a level playing field. Which leads to balance of payment issues, and the ever-reliance on the crutch of a Rupee in perennial decline. I see no way out, unless the collective west treats India like Israel. India’s revolution of the mind hasn’t happened yet.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: The US has no more technologies to put sanctions against China. As for the Chinese-made products such as the world most advances Huawei 5G, smartphones, solar energy panels, China made EVs, shipbuildings etc are 100% Chinese technologies. Why?
Answer: I’d like to give a short and oblique answer. In one word, margin. In one sentence: the curse of quarterly earnings. The whole problem with American manufacturing is margin, because of skyrocketing cost and paradoxically, expectation. Look at the magnificent 7. They are all, to a fault, either internet or chip giants with sky-high IP- or service monopoly-enabled margins and valuations. Unfortunately, the backbone of the economy isn’t high-tech, or high margin. The only way they could survive was to lower cost, and find new revenue streams. They solved the first problem by relocating out of America, and the second partly by selling to the rest of the world. This was why globalization became such a buzzword, because rich Western media trumpeted the model. For a few decades, everyone benefited, until the internet boom threw balance sheet expectations out of whack. Investors not only demanded dividends, but also capital appreciation, and the stock buyback became mandatory in the 21st century. Intel for example spent in excess of 100b on stock buyback this century, and it hasn’t had a leading edge node chip for almost a decade. Unions and collective bargaining wrecked havoc on company finances and HR turnover. Just ask GM, which is still paying down pension commitments dating pre-GFC. Elon is adamant about a no-union Tesla, and has taken aggression action against unionization. Otherwise, it would have faced immense blowback in its recent retrenchment exercise. Meanwhile, CEO compensation have been shooting for the moon, and THE KPI to meet is the company’s stock price. The easiest way is to sell sexy growth stories for the public to stomach inflated earning multiples. In a world where the global competition is rapidly catching up and with few greenfield markets left to exploit, margin expansion requires cost-cutting. Which explains Boeing’s woes today, letting go of senior engineers, and allowing standards to slip, while contracting away key components that Boeing used to make inhouse. One final example. The loyalty program of Delta Airlines is worth more than its market value. In other words, the equity value of physical airline operation (planes, brand, landing slots) is negative. Understand how loyalty miles turn a profit for airlines and you’ll have the answer to the question posed. It’s over-financialization, and the stock market, silly.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: After Yellen's visit to China, the USTR initiates a Section 301 investigation into China's maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors. How to interpret the U.S. move? What are the implications?
Answer: It’s here: The first PDF link on the page. The meat begins on page 112. The rest can be skipped, although I must admit it was professionally put together in some parts. I’ll save the reader some time by going directly to the main remedy sought: the imposition of a tariff on China-built ships docking in US ports. But what’s a politically driven policy without a juicy soundbite? A cool million dollars per ship docking, at a minimum, scaling with the size. At ~10,000 ships per year throughput, that’s $10b annually, injected into a U.S. Commercial Shipbuilding Revitalization Fund. There are exemptions baked in for China-made vessels in the Maritime Security Program (“MSP”) and Tanker Security Program (TSP). The petition also targets the deployment and utilization of China’s LOGINK logistic system, calling on the U.S. and friends to restrict and end its use in existing ports. The petitioners? 4 unions (predominantly older white men) and 1 Federal department. Which means most of the money will be funneled to pension funds and benefits. Note: Donald’s blanket tariffs have netted way more, with hundreds of billions generated for federal coffers over the past few years. I’m pretty sure charging blanket tariffs based on the carrying vessel’s country of manufacture is unprecedented, and probably illegal under WTO rules. But since Donald has already implemented unprecedented blanket tariffs on goods of Chinese origin (which has been continued by 2 separate administrations), this is no surprise. So much for global cooperation and “alliances” to contain China, and another public slap at the “rules-based order”. The impact isn’t too great economically speaking, because the ~20% blanket tariffs on most Chinese imports is worth 10x more to the Fed. Politically, this will win votes at the Union level, and among the MAGA crowd. The cost, though, will be born by the American consumer. It isn’t clear to me how Pacific shipping flow will be reshaped, yet. But I’d say the penalties, if passed, will benefit American unions and Korean/Japanese shipbuilding. Which is probably the unspoken thrust of this charade, oops, investigation.

Question: Who is Reporters Without Borders (RSF)? Why 2 RSF reporters were questioned by HK authority (at airport) on 2024/4/10? At the end, MS A Bielakowska was denied entry to HK. Another one was allowed entry but voluntarily left HK the next day.

The United States Customs turn people away on a daily basis, from tourists who “look suspicious” or speak little or no English, to students carrying valid visas. Hong Kong rarely reject arrivals. That’s why the above made the news. Many foreign NGOs and “free press” journalists have left Hong Kong since the enactment of the National Security Law. There appears to be a second wave of departures with the enactment of the recent upgrade, patching holes in the legal framework. Why? The legal advice is the significantly increased risk of getting into trouble, particularly the bread and butter issue of funding. The strategy is to convert permanent city presence to rotating short term trips to stir the waters, using neighboring cities such as Taipei as bases of operation. Instead of answering the question directly (What they are isn’t important), I’d like to end with a poser. Would RSF pull the same stunt in Singapore, say to cover our elections? Would NGOs and the “free press” relocate to Singapore to cover Hong Kong? Why?

Question: Do you think Chinese leaders believe US criticisms of China's excess capacity in some industries are in bad faith?
Answer: This isn't pencils or notebooks we are talking about. These are products such as solar panels and EVs that can easily cost five figures or more. Any plant making such products anywhere in the world will require significant local government assistance, such as land use, utilities, and supporting infrastructure. These are de-facto subsidies, and deals often involve direct subsidies, such as Nevada’s >$1b grant for Tesla’s gigafactory a decade back. Why? They bring stable, long-term jobs to the community. In addition, governments around the world have to subsidize the enabling infrastructure, such as upgrading power management in the existing grid to accommodate fluctuating solar/wind/green energy generation, and adding power stations and building charging networks for EVs. These are massive public subsidies, and it happens around the world. However, tax driven overcapacity is an oxymoron, simply because these industries burn through capital at the speed of light. Take EVs. Every 100k overcapacity of a $10k car is a $1b timebomb on the balance sheet. Not only that, unsold inventory incur costs. What happens in such situations is initial stockpiling of excess inventory, followed by inevitable production cuts through man hour reduction and if it persists, layoffs. This is what we observe in Tesla recently—burgeoning unsold inventory, reduced production, and finally layoffs. But that isn’t happening in Tesla Shanghai, which is adding significant production capacity. It remains the only gigafactory worldwide driving Tesla’s quarterly earnings. It is the same story with the other firms accused of “over-capacity”. They are all expanding rapidly, because the demand is there. For example, China recently installed more solar panels in one year than America has in its entire history. Ask Elon why Shanghai is expanding while there are layoffs and burgeoning inventory elsewhere. It’s politics, and prejudice.

Question: What historical basis do any of the claimants to the South China Sea islands have?
Answer: I will provide the barest framework for further exploration of the interested reader. Let’s list the claimant states with disputes in the SCS. Vietnam, Malaysia, Philippines, Brunei and China. Indonesia isn’t a claimant. Japan isn’t a claimant. Australia isn’t a claimant. NATO, Quad and AUKAS members are not claimants. With the exception of Indonesia, the rest of the busybodies have committed MILITARY assets towards the dispute, and have threatened the use of force on the issue, despite China securing and maintaining an agreement among all claimants to deploy ONLY coast guard assets without lethal arms, as they work towards an SCS code of conduct. Now, what is sovereignty, in the modern context? It is based on history, and the means of enforcing RECOGNITION of continuity. Case in point: the state of Palestine, which has strong historical claim, but has been blocked from recognition by the powers that be for generations. Plenty of colonial-era excesses remain, despite the retreat of empire post-WWII. For example, there are two pieces of Spain (Europe) in Morocco (Africa), pieces of the UK in the Caribbean (off Central America), South Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Polynesia, pieces of France in Polynesia, the Caribbean, the North Atlantic, Indian Ocean, even South America proper, and pieces of the US in the Caribbean, and Western Pacific. None of these can be explained by geographic contiguity, or UNCLOS. In fact, many look ridiculous on political maps. They are remnants of colonialism, and clear reminders of white people’s dark history. Now, the crux of the South China Sea dispute hinges on one determination. Do the claims predate WWII, or not? If the answer is yes, then China’s claim is rock solid, and supported by one simple observation. Before WWII, none of the other claimant states existed—they were all colonies for hundreds of years, and NONE OF THEM made claims to the islands/features in the SCS. Whereas China under the Qing/Ming did, and there are historical records and maps to support the claim. Is the PRC the legitimate heir to the Qing? Well, the Chinese people decided that long ago. The PRC government caused a furor when it released a 9-dash line map some years ago. But it merely referenced an 11-dash line map that Taipei released WITH THE BLESSING of Macarthur the Shogun’s Japan administration. The map was surveyed with the immense resources of the USN, and it was an update to an even older map, the 13-dash line Qing map of the SCS. The problem is the muddied history introduced by the treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895, when Qing China ceded Taiwan to Japan as part of war reparation, and the subsequent renouncement of Japan’s rights to Taiwan post-WWII defeat. Taiwan’s status today is unsettled, just like Palestine, blocked from resolution by the powers that be. Without the question of Taiwan, there will be no need for the SCS debacle today. P.S.: The Bonins have been “returned” to Japan since 1968. The archipelago is >1,000km from Tokyo, and the main harbor is a full day’s fast ship-ride away. Anyone screaming UNCLOS and spitting on Japan?

Question: I'm from India. How can India and China resolve it's border issue without blaming each other for a greater good of Asian dominance. Only positive comments from both sides please?
Answer: Ever since Jawaharlal’s overreach, China has stringently kept to the negotiated bargain struck through numerous rounds of talks. That includes no firearms on border patrols, and mutual retreat from the disputed border, creating a no-man’s land buffer. Unfortunately, India decided to unilaterally upset the hard-won status quo by introducing settlers, and upgrading connectivity, making inroads into no-man’s land. The pace has accelerated alarmingly in the 21st century. The Chinese mirrored Indian development, but managed to do so at a faster clip than the Indians, particularly east of the vulnerable chicken’s neck. This caused the Indians to break longstanding protocol, when armed Indian troops entered Doklam in 2017 to stop Chinese troops from constructing a road. That could have easily led to war. Provocation been escalating for years along many parts of the India-China behavior, and isn’t confined to the Mcmahon line. India needs a strong leader to walk back on Jawaharlal’s legacy, and admit the strategic overreach. Unfortunately, his status as the father of Indian democracy prevents the polity from disavowing its past, just like the Chrysanthemum throne’s iron grip on Japanese history. I see no way out, and I expect the border issue to be milked for political effect periodically, like what we witnessed during covid. China is willing to sit down and negotiate any time.

Question: What challenges do you think Apple will face in regaining its position as the top phonemaker, especially with the rise of Chinese brands like Huawei and Xiaomi?
Answer: Steve, before he died, characterized Apple’s strategy to be the “Mercedes of smartphones/computing”. Mercedes isn’t the top carmaker by volume. It can’t be, by definition, if its catchment is the premium end of the market. Apple shipping the number of phones it did the past few years is an historical aberration that will be corrected and has been correcting. Unless Tim walks back on Steve’s words and converts to a “Toyota of smartphones/computing” strategy, there is no way back, not when there is plenty of wriggle room in terms of margin for the competition to exploit. Besides, Apple doesn’t make anything. It is a client of contract manufacturing, and dependent on the ecosystem for hardware innovation. The competition is rapidly evolving and the landscape is shifting. Huawei has introduced cutting edge products that is largely free from western technology. It even has its own software stack that has a mature IOT implementation at the kernel level. This will pose significant challenge to Apple’s iOS/Mac ecosystem in the coming decade, as Huawei begins to write next-gen hardware standards, as well as the pivot of the hardware component supply chain away from the west. In other words, what will Apple do when it shops around 5–10 years into the future and find the best cameras, sensors, batteries, screens, glass, 6g modems, NFC/short range wireless, space comms, even CPU/GPU/NPU are ALL Chinese?

Question: Sr. American Diplomat Kurt Campbell stated that the USA will hold China accountable for Russia's territorial gains in Ukraine. What is the Chinese thoughts on this matter? Is the USA overstepping it's authority?
Answer: Heard about six degrees of separation? This was one of the problems I came across studying Monte Carlo simulations. Six degrees of separation is a rule of thumb that all people are six or fewer social connections away from each other. What does it have to do with Kurt the Assistant Secretary of State? It has all to do with holding the Chinese accountable for Russia’s actions in Ukraine. The answer lies in secondary sanctions, which is a historic expansion of the big sanction stick enabled by the hegemonic hold of the Eurodollar over the global economy.  How did sanctions work? America would draw up a list of companies to sanction, and depending on the severity of the sanction, make it illegal for American companies to trade with companies A, B, and C or kick them entirely from the dollar system. This works because of the unnatural size of the US economy, and the requirement for all dollar-based transactions to be cleared through NYC. That’s direct sanction. America is introducing secondary sanctions on Russia, to sanction partners that trade with companies A, B and C. This bears a little explaining. Say companies D, E, and F trade with the three amigos above. Under the old sanction model, their Eurodollar transactions with other parties won’t be affected. But under secondary sanctions, these transactions will be subject to the same sanction. In other words, collective punishment, or guilt by association. For example, India will find it difficult to resell Russian energy to Europe because the Indian energy company will be subject to the same sanctions as the Russian energy company, and it will affect their Eurodollar business with European customers. Two, a second degree social map will expand the list of sanctioned entities by multiples, if not an order of magnitude. That’s a snowball rolling downhill, in terms of ...

The highly purified specialist inputs such as wafers, chemicals and interconnects are rapidly coming online, especially on mature nodes. Significant progress had been made to codify this into a Code of Conduct for the SCS, until the recent U-turn by the Philippines under Bong Bong. Militarizing the issue (especially the appearance of significant military assets from non-claimants), as well as escalating provocation by the Philippines can only herald the appearance of the Chinese military, and not just in the SCS, but also Diaoyutai. Tear up the gentlemen’s agreement and it’s knuckledusters at the cul de sac in the fading dusk. I won’t be surprised if naval assets are boomed by low-flying jets, or warning shots fired across the bow. Further, I expect casualties, if the provocation is overplayed. It’s a politically charged year, and if 2020 was anything to go by, we can expect the Americans to pull some outlandish moves.

Question: The US has been two to three generations behind of the Chinese hypersonic missiles and technologies. What is the US going to to do about it?

I’m not optimistic, given the dearth of clean-sheet designs fielded by the US military this century, and the inability to ramp up the production of basic war materiel such as artillery shells recently. Name: Bill Chen
Question: Who pays the costs of de-linking and de-coupling supply chains from Chinese suppliers and manufacturers, and friend-shoring new supply chains to countries friendly to the west?
Answer: Good question. Unfortunately, this requires a nuanced answer to explore properly. I’ll sprinkle a few crumbs to help the reader frame the issue, and identify possible avenues of exploration. Manufacturing, especially in the first world, is no longer the exclusive model of vertical integration, where brands ship end product from raw material processed in self-owned factories. Today’s manufacturing is horizontal. Many brands (especially consumer goods) form supplier eco-systems, and may even leave final assembly to contract manufacturers. The most famous example is Apple, whose manufacturing department consists of PMs, accountants and lawyers. Tim Cook got rid of Apple’s factories, and reduced its inventory from months to days. Cash flow is what it takes to thrive at the pinnacle of tech. Now, how does a business model like Apple friend-shore when it doesn’t own the physical supply chain? We hear the press painting developments as “Apple leaves China for India”, but in reality, it is Chinese (more accurately, Taiwanese contract manufacturers) being offered incentives by Apple to set up production in India. This is the same story with TSMC and Samsung, with Apple (and other customers) dangling premium-laden contracts and/or financing to reshape the flow of manufacturing. But that’s often just the labor-intensive assembly portion. The rest of the horizontal supply chain stays put in East Asia, especially the R&D and toolmaking. The assembly process is also developed and tested in China, before being farmed out beyond the mainland. This is the only way to guarantee the extremely tight product cycles that Apple adheres to. Now, who pays for friend-shoring Apple? The customers of course. Apple though, can afford to pad the exercise with a minor margin shrink, as long as it doesn’t involve wholesale uprooting of the existing supply chain. There is another cost to friendshoring—the loss of mainland consumer appeal, especially Apple designating India-assembled iphones for the mainland market, despite the premium the Chinese pay compared to Japan or stateside. Witness Dell and Apple’s plummeting market share among the Chinese. Mixing business with politics is not only potent, but toxic. The operating buzz-word for Apple, Dell, HP and others in this capex-heavy exercise is the ubiquitous “AI”, allowing companies to keep their stock price up even when revenue is down and expenditure up. Got to give it to the Americans, for delivering a massive lesson in economic psyops. There are other avenues to explore different business models, but this will suffice for now.

Question: How much support is there among the BRICS member states to Russia's proposal to set up a BRICS grain exchange to coordinate food production policy?
Answer: India won’t support it, because it violates the tenets of Indian centrality, which is the overarching theme of the Narendra administration. India is the world’s largest rice exporter, and surprise surprise, the second largest beef exporter worldwide, despite persistently ranking 10th percentile on the World Hunger Index. India will not want to chain itself to policy that can affect its balance of payment and forex inflow. China is a net food importer, particularly feed grains for livestock. It also imports grains to maintain the world’s most extensive grain reserve program, to guarantee price stability and availability. The rest of the imports satisfy lucrative niche demand. It is Brazil, Russia and future members that will benefit from coordination, but especially Brazil. The last time I looked, Brazil grew enough soy in 2023/24 to fully supply both its domestic consumption and China’s (50+100m tonnes), which is a remarkable figure. Unfortunately, China has committed to resource diversification and will not buy everything from one country. Amazingly, soy prices have held up despite the bumper increase, so there must be adjustments elsewhere in the market. Russia wants to wrest control of that price-making power from the west, particularly America, whose farmers have been known to destroy crop and fallow land to keep grain prices high and generate artificial shortage. The card I believe Russia is playing is the warming of Siberia, and the reclaiming of vast stretches of fertile black tundra soil every year as the glaciers retreat. Russian food production can potentially shoot for the moon in the coming decades, and there is enormous export potential, because of Russia’s small population. In essence, Russia wants to bring other major producers in to regulate its developing market-making power to create a sustainable eco-system free from the tyranny of first world commodity pricing. I may update this after picking the mind of my commodity trading friend. But that may take time.
