Name: Bill Chen
Question: With China's extremely different culture and values from the west is democracy simply impossible to achieve? Is authoritarianism the natural solution for a successful and prosperous China?
Answer: Democracy as in one man one vote? The Chinese use that to choose leaders at the grassroots level (classrooms, committees, villages) where the people know and interact with each other on a daily basis. On bigger scales, one man one vote hasn’t worked, despite numerous Chinese experiments to tweak the process. Even on smaller scales, one man one vote has been subject to abuse, particularly corruption and abuse of power at the village level. Billion-yuan cases and father-son leadership transition scandals have been uncovered in recent years. Fundamentally, the argument in the Anglophone media is one of legitimacy. Only western-style liberal democracy is legitimate. Any country that deviates from the gold standard of rich nordic democracy is either deficient, or worse, illegitimate. That’s the entire purpose of the extravagantly maintained Democracy Index by the Economist, and countless human rights NGOs, funded no doubt to further political aims. America has already given the world vivid lessons about the rules-based international order, and Gina is far from the only teacher in the room. Exclude China and exclude your country from the EV revolution, just like drones, photovoltaics, 6g and many other standards of tomorrow. China is democratizing technology, and the global south will have first dips in a game American doesn’t want in. Chinese consumers can buy 4-wheel EVs with climate control today for ¥30–35,000, or $4–5,000. What’s the floor for an EV stateside? $30–40k? That’s a 7–8x differential. Eventually, America will be forced to come to the table, because the Chinese have the most complete and competitive EV eco-system anywhere in the world.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: China sets the 2024 GDP growth target at around 5%. How do you view this target?
Answer: That means more air can be potentially let out of the real estate bubble. In other words, harsher pace of drawdown compared to 2023 is on the cards, if the external environment remains stable. Why? This is a dragon year, and births have picked up. Babies are expensive, the single greatest household expenditure after mortgage payments. There is more wriggle room to shrink real estate GDP contribution, provided macro conditions don’t deteriorate. 5% is a reasonable figure, and the consensus I picked up from mainland friends.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Will a US sanction on BYD be more or less effective than on Huawei?
Answer: Which piece of American technology is crucial to BYD’s EV? In different words, which American patent/s is/are key to enabling a BYD EV? The American government’s gatekeeper right to the use of American owned patents is the key legal argument used to deny technology to Huawei and its ecosystem of suppliers, down to the tools used in design and manufacturing. That is how America is forcing Dutch, German, Taiwanese, Japanese and Korean firms from doing business with Huawei. The problem with EVs ex-China is the lack of focus, with the exception of Tesla. Unfortunately, even Tesla failed to turn a profit until their Shanghai factory came online. And every EV produced beyond China is either loss-making, or prohibitively expensive, even with subsidies thrown in. Scale-up is impossible without Chinese help. Case in point: a VW ID6 sells for €16,000 in China, and €40,000 back home in Germany. That’s the status quo, which can be summarized as China having a HUGE lead in the EV world compared to the rest. We are not talking about a lead in components, or software. China has achieved DOMINANCE of the entire EV supply chain, from raw materials, to AI and self-driving. I was chatting with a mainland friend who is based in Shenzhen. He is a car enthusiast, and spends his weekends test-driving and posting mini-reviews on his social media channel. When the Mercedes EQS debuted, I asked “what do you think?” He laughed and said, “it’s a Mercedes, but specs-wise, there are no selling points.” In other words, the EQS platform architecture is only world-class beyond Chinese shores. I won’t elaborate, because I’d rather the reader do his own research and marvel at the profundity of the truth captured by the above sentence. Gina and co. will be denying inferior technology (and that includes the toolmaking) that China has little use for, were they to pull a Huawei on BYD. I’ll end with three anecdotes. Alibaba makes cars. Yes, Alibaba the e-commerce and mobile payment giant. One model offers wireless charging. Yes, WIRELESS CHARGING that escape even laptops. Li Auto, a name most may not have heard of, debuted an MPV recently that is capable of >550kw fast charging. That is equal to 10–80% of a 100kwh battery or adding 400km range in 10 minutes. Puts Tesla’s “Supercharger” to shame doesn’t it? This is the future of EVs—the $4–5,000 4-wheel scooter/motorbike, with a roof and climate control. Edit: From Prasant Sharma, who has an Economics Degree from the 1980s, which makes him an elite Indian of the era. Says a lot, doesn’t it? Producers of cheap products or products with normal technology are dependent upon the consumers and not the other way around. There are hundreds of ev car manufacturers in the world. Chinese car has no speciality except it's cheap price. No country in the world would allow the unrestricted amount of cheap products if it adversely affect the welfare of their manufacturers/ ultimately consumers/ country. USA is the biggest car market. China is an Authoritarian country which manipulates the prices of its products (as was the case with API market in India where first it dumped it's API products and when the Indian API manufacturers closed down, Chinese increased their prices manifold). Only Chinese vasal states would allow unlimited access to the Chinese products. For a long term business relationship, ultimately Chinese have to accept parity between it's imports and exports. Soon the Chinese understand, better it would be for them.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Are American tanks rubbish?
Answer: Compared to other tanks, no. But in terms of current production numbers and cost, it offers little bang for buck, and it will be hard to expand capacity to fill orders. That said, the ongoing revolution on the battlefield requires constant adaptation and innovation. The Russians have dispersed their armor columns into smaller units, with drone and anti-drone detachments attached. Unit tactics have pivoted entirely to drone operation, in defense and attack. Traditional armor doctrine of massed columns (even with artillery and air dominance) will not fare well against such opposition. This is the essence of the arms race, technology enabling measures, and countermeasures. The tank needs a radical rethink in the age of autonomous weapons. Personally, I believe the age of the gun is over, with smart munitions and robots taking over. But that’s just me.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: I heard the Chinese government doesn't pay salaries but supplies food and other things to the citizens. Is that true, and if true, does it mean there is no needy in China?
Answer: There are ~10 million civil servants out of a labor pool of 800m. These 10 million employees of the government are all paid wages, and on retirement, pensions for life. My friend’s dad is a retired policeman. He receives his pension regularly, and he and his wife travel every year when the grandchildren are away. The days of food coupons is long over, though old-timers still know what they are. Food and necessities were given out as compensation in the old days but this has been replaced by salary.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: What do you think of Beijing's accusation that Taiwan used "violent and dangerous methods" during an incident that led to the deaths of two mainland Chinese fishermen?
Answer: First, the incident happened in broad daylight, around noon of February 14th, the fifth day of Chinese New Year. The sea was calm, and weather good, on one of the slowest days of the year. The boat in question was pleasure-craft size, and not a commercial fishing boat. Of the 4 men on board, two survived and have been released back to the mainland. They have given statements to both the authorities and media. What the survivors and Taiwanese authorities corroborate is there was a chase, and the small boat was repeatedly rammed FROM BEHIND by the Coast Guard until it capsized, causing the death of two. The incident went unreported despite the fatalities for 5–7 days. Repeat attempts by the mainland to obtain information about the missing men came back empty. After the story finally broke, the account from Taiwanese authorities has repeatedly shifted with each media update and clarification. What is undeniable is a stream of lies and omissions being fed to the public, with officials inventing new lies to cover up old ones that run into logical cul-de-sacs. Plenty of doubt remain. For example, why must the bodies be forcefully cremated without an open/joint autopsy? Even the bodies of executed prisoners are claimed by families, what more a couple of trespassers a stone’s throw away from xiamen? Are there bullets in the bodies or mangled body parts? Next, why is there no video or audio record of the chase, but there are pre-chase and post-chase recordings? Recording is an established operational requirement, and not doing so invites discipline. What about surface radar plots, which the Coast Guard must possess? And so on. It’s a sham and complete coverup. The mainland has no choice but to take the survivors at their word, and it doesn’t look good for Taiwan. And in a might is right game, Taiwan does not need to turn up.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: US Abrams tanks have been destroyed in Ukraine, does that mean US tanks are not game changers as was hoped?
Answer: Sending Abrams is just an PR exercise to demonstrate “the Americans are coming!” Just like the Challenger to demonstrate “the Brits are coming!” Their presence in Ukraine was supposed to part the red… urm… black sea. The Ukrainian conflict is being fought along a proper front hundreds of kilometers long, and for the first time in a long while, no side has complete air dominance. This makes for exciting doctrinal development, especially in combined arms, and total warfare, the system of systems integration that is the foundation of modern war. Put simply, this is nothing but a rehashing of the millennia-old question generals have always asked. How far can I see, and how far can I hit? Unfortunately, a new chapter of warfare is being written by drones and autonomous robots, rendering traditional weapons like armor vulnerable. Tanks were not designed to counter threats from the sky, especially cheap kamikaze drones that have the ability to loiter for hours and detect, identify and destroy targets autonomously/via data link. The drone is changing armor doctrine for good. Putting a big gun on a tracked turret within range of a cheap drone is suicidal today, for the simple reason the gun can’t hurl projectiles further than the drone can fly. Superweapons? Game-changers? Nah.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Why can Ferrari not be driven daily?
Answer: Well, there was a red Ferrari that was a daily commuter parked at an outdoor carpark here. Urban tropics, with world-class road system. Plenty of humps, but no potholes. I know the owner in passing, who bought it brand new. The daily commute was no more than 20km, from home and back. Cost aside, the car started looking worse for wear within the first few years. Far as I know, it was carefully driven and never been in an accident. The headlamp cover developed cracks within the first year, and began to cloud over by the second. The paint lost its gloss, and there were problems with the locks, power windows, battery and hydraulics. The agent told the owner the engine was generating too much heat, and the murderous tropical weather and humidity was taking a toll. Parts availability and service delays were also headaches...

Name: Bill Chen
Question: A rhetoric has emerged recently in some Western countries, which claims that China's comparative strength, or its economy, is peaking. What's the arguments for the so-called "Peak China"? How do you view it?
Answer: Peak China is simply a superimposition of late 80s/90s Japan onto today’s China. Popping asset bubble, shrinking and aging population, debt troubles, FDI drop, sanctions, dehumanization, stock market crash… The whole nine yards. I won’t bother with a flyby, because the Zeihans and Pettises of the world are doing a much better job pumping the collapse. In 2001, when China first ascended the WTO after a decades-long negotiation process, “a billion pairs of socks for an airliner” was still a popular refrain in the Chinese consciousness. 2001 isn’t too long ago. It was the year 9.11 happened, and also the year the forever war OF terror began. In 2024, this is what a modern Chinese factory looks like. Rows and rows of robots churning out thousands dollar battery packs like clockwork, driven by high speed networks, multiple sensors and AI-assisted fault-tolerant control. In 2001, I didn’t remember seeing any Chinese booths at the Singapore Air Show. Today, there are military and commercial offerings aplenty, including the C919, China’s answer to the narrowbody dominance of the A320 and B737. I have not checked but according to friends, BYD is able to begin risk production in its foreign factories within 12–18 months of the lease being signed, and ramp up to full production within 18 months of operation. BYD’s EV production is a radically different model to the Japanese and German ICE lines, and the progress is breathtaking, particularly the upstream control/access to tools and raw materials. In telecoms, Huawei is deploying 5.5G networks, with 10x the speed of 5G, with 5.5G modems on the device side playing catchup. Qualcomm may find itself licensing Huawei designs if it isn’t careful to keep up. Huawei has patents that cover the entire stack from server, network to device. There is immense potential of bandwidth enabling revolutions in industry and autonomous self-driving. Huawei’s comeback Mate 60 is selling very well, affecting Apple’s China shipments, down 30% yoy. The P70 is also attracting lots of attention pre-release. How much of the lost 200 million shipped volume will Huawei reclaim this year? On to chips. There are many fabs under construction today, from legacy to advanced nodes. China will make half the world’s chip by 2030, and conceivably becoming a net chip exporter within the next decade. This from a position of spending more on chip import than oil recently. China has achieved commercial availability of the world’s first gas-cooled 4th gen nuclear power plant, after passing years of stringent grid testing. The rest of the competition don’t even have a test reactor today, so the Chinese lead is a good 10–15 years. Can you imagine a world where the global south (or the 150 countries in the BRI) enjoy pockets of technology that is more affordable and better yet, cutting edge wrt the global north? That day is coming, if not the 2030s, then certainly the 2040s. That’s Chinese democratization for you. Whatever you think of the Chinese, they are just getting started.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: China’s GDP growth was 5 . 2 % in 2023. What about its economic momentum in 2024?
Answer: I won’t be surprised if Premier Li announces a similar 5% growth target this year at the two meetings, due to external uncertainties. The collective west needs a financial reset after the irresponsible money-printing over the past few years. For example, the US GDP was 21 trillion in 2019. It’s 27 trillion today (early 2024), or 6 trillion increase. That’s an increase of 1.5 trillion a year on average, in a society embroiled in massive death, and a huge decrease in live births and marriage, dipping to multi-decade lows. Electricity generation has dropped, while crime, overdose, and homelessness are on the up. Does that sound like an economy that has innovated its way to a 6 trillion increase in 4 years? Europe, or at least the prosperous parts, are mired in recession and energy subsidy hell, courtesy of Nordstream and Ukraine. Japan is similarly battling recession and real wage depression, while both the Dax and Nikkei are printing record highs. It’s a mad, mad world isn’t it, with the average folk worried about the price of groceries, rent and winter heat, while long waitlists discourage shoppers from Rolex sports watches. Yes, it’s an election year, but economic forces are hard to contain once unleashed, and the hands of central bankers are tied—they cannot accommodate more without inflation rearing its ugly head again. My friends have their doubts about 2024, and I share many of their concerns. I’d rather China print a 5% target and increase live births above 14 million, rather than growth at all cost. The past few years have taken a tremendous toll on Chinese family life.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Why does Singapore's birth rate continue to fall despite the use of financial incentives?
Answer: Covid. Birth rates in the first world have plunged, and only immigration is keeping numbers pretty. SMEs have taken the brunt of the balance sheet devastation, and jobs have been lost, exacerbated by inflation of goods, services, and assets. Singapore is no different. Things are stabilizing, and we will see better numbers, as long as the West doesn’t implode.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: How does China's crackdown on consulting firms reflect growing tensions with the United States?
Answer: In the latest McDonald’s quarterly call, the company revealed it opened >1,000 restaurants in mainland China in 2023, making it the fastest growing market globally. 1,000 restaurants is 3 per DAY, and McDonald’s is about as American as any brand can be. China’s policing of consultancies is merely a rounding error, in the grand scheme of corporate America. Annually, the S&P 500 generate >$1 trillion in revenue operating within the mainland market. This includes Apple, which depend on China for 20–25% of its global revenue. How much are these consultancies worth? A couple of million each? What’s happening is the CIA’s doubling down on intelligence within China, as traditional humint sources were vacuumed up in the repeated corruption sweeps since Xi took charge. These consultancies have served as spy centers and information conduits, but were allowed to operate in deference of American hegemony. But relationships have become frazzled and the cases linked to these nodes made them intolerable. Actual cases are being pursued, and people are being prosecuted, with a number deported rather than risk diplomatic protest. America is preparing for war, and it shows in the information they are willing to pay for, particularly the networks and capabilities they are willing to risk. Case in point: What was a Seawolf-class attack sub doing in the SCS, only to suffer a head-on collision with an undersea mount?

Name: Bill Chen
Question: How did India cross China’s population in 2024? Does india's low GDP per capita (2.8) with 140th rank can even get worse further in the future?
Answer: The top 3 most populous countries today (2024) is in the following order: India, China, USA. Now, would it be surprising to find the Chinese labor pool is 1 India + 2 Americas? In different words, India lags China by 300m jobs, and forces India to be the number 1 exporter of labor worldwide, contributing wage repatriation equal to 2–3+% of Indian GDP. 300 MILLION jobs, at a time when more than half (800m) of the Indian population is on government-sponsored food subsidy. How did India increase its population? Subsidies, not jobs. I have friends who live in India, or stayed previously. Life is very comfortable for the upper middle class, because hired help is cheap, and service provision in cities is extraordinary, perhaps unmatched anywhere else today. Why? Labor is cheap, especially the low-skill hired help. The service industry can afford the luxury of employing 2 or more workers for each position and still turn a nice profit. One Indian friend calls it tailored consumer pampering, and he isn’t far off the mark. But all that points to a society that does not have enough jobs, with the decades-long capital account struggles and the perennial slide of the rupee ample evidence of the malaise. After all, what does a devaluing rupee imply about Indian labor? Not cheap enough. In the age of AI, many skilled jobs will be lost or downsized, what more the unskilled/low skilled? Many will turn into the “useless class”, as Yuval Noah Harari puts it. Plenty of Indians, especially those on food subsidies, will face massive challenges eking a living in the future. More isn’t better. More may equal disaster in the making. This is a modern Chinese car factory. It’s robots, robots everywhere. How many humans are needed to make a million cars like that? India’s demographics entrenches structural poverty, for the next generation at the very least, and the headache of excess labor will be exacerbated by the technological revolution. Add in climate change and ecological damage to South Asia and India has plenty on her plate. The shifts in the snow melts of the Himalayas is also cause for concern. India will continue to grow from its low base. But my Indian friend’s observation rings true. “India is rushing towards a future she is ill-prepared for.”

Name: Bill Chen
Question: If China and Taiwan agreed to a peaceful reunification, how would the USA respond to the situation?
Answer: It is 2024. The Prime Minister of the East Turkistan Government-in-Exile claims sovereignty over this map. The registered address of the government he leads is a stone’s throw from DC 20004. In fact, his government was declared within the august halls of the Capitol two decades ago, in 2004. Just like Russia, China is too big, too powerful to be left alone. If Xinjiang’s secession can be actively promoted (but not officially supported) by American leaders, consent for Taiwan’s reunification is “over my dead body”. Look at Cuba. 30+ consecutive UNGA resolutions have failed to end Cuba’s embargo, and they are yet again in danger of suffering food shortages. America will need to weaken geopolitically for peaceful reunification to happen. That or lose convincingly under a hail of bullets and bombs. Note: There is another Goverrnment-in-Exile, based permanently in Dharamsala, India. Imagine, a direct neighbor sharing a border sheltering (but not officially supporting) a secessionist government for 60+ years. I wonder what India will say to Punjab, Manipur and Kashmir governments-in-exile setting up shop in Beijing—and elsewhere. Send more assassins?

Name: Bill Chen
Question: When did the collective West start to freak out about the rise of China from being positive?
Answer: Shortly after the GFC. Why? Hillary pleaded with China to help stabilize the dollar and the American government debt market. Pointedly, the newly appointed Secretary of State made a huge political statement by kickstarting her 100+ country travel circuit with Beijing. China not only committed to buying Federal debt, but it also expanded fiscal spending on a massive scale, doubling down on infrastructure. Chinese growth and monetary injection helped pad the fallout from the GFC, which saw the dollar devalue by more than 30%. American leaders belatedly awoke to the fact that China was already a mover and shaker, just because of the rarefied size of the Chinese economy. The yuan issued by the world’s second largest economy hasn’t ascended to the table, still dominated by 4 currencies: dollar, euro, yen, pound. That’s the sole reason why the G7 remains relevant today: financial dominance. Let’s go back to 2012, when Barack was campaigning for his second term, having stabilized the American economy. What was the platform he campaigned on? The pivot to Asia. Let me repeat, because this is a pivotal moment in 21st century geopolitics. THE PIVOT TO ASIA. Or rather, a thinly veiled platform to fix China and the Chinese. The most consequential strategy that arose out of the pivot is a known fact that rarely surfaces in discussions. I call it the Reverse Plaza Accord. After winning his second term, Barack and the G7 essentially gave the BOJ carte blanche to devalue the yen, then held to captive highs as the darling of the carry trade. The rest of the third world followed the yen’s lead, and devalued massively, with one notable absentee: China. Both the Barack and Donald administrations relentlessly attacked the PBOC’s monetary policy, threatening sanctions for currency manipulation. Singapore was drawn into the mess for operating a similar exchange rate mechanism based on the BBC (Basket, Band and Crawl), managed against a basket of currencies of major trading partners, and threatened with designation in tandem. The political message (for those in the know) was crystal clear: do not devalue the yuan to keep pace with the rest. What was the goal? Give Japan an unfair forex edge at high tech exports, while forcing low-tech exports out of China to the rest of the third world. Notice the flattening/dip of ex-china cost post-2013? That’s the reverse plaza accord, measured in dollars. Barack was using American hegemony to enforce step change in the forces shaping the Chinese economy. China lost plenty of jobs—and babies—over the past decade. But what did Beijing do? It hunkered down, bit its tongue, and decided to focus on home renovation. Let’s transit from unbridled expansion to quality and HSE (Health, Safety, Environment). Let’s focus on domestic recirculation and develop OBOR markets rather than chase first world exports. Let’s pursue indigenous technology rather than buy foreign. Let’s pivot from the West, too. The discipline was merciless, and there were pockets of carnage in the upheaval. For example, opportunities in the Northeast—long a major industrial heart—became so limited the migration of entrepreneurs west to Yunnan and elsewhere was promoted and facilitated by the government. The yuan has hardly moved the past decade, hovering around a 10–15% band of 6.6 to the dollar. The rest of the third world and Japan have all corrected lower. In the yen’s case, a 100% devaluation. How does China remain the world’s factory with a 300% rise in labor cost within a decade? Or in other words, how does China remain competitive with externally-imposed margin squeeze? That’s a topic worthy of a book-length dive. Pacific Command is now Indopacom. The annual APEC summit is now a backburner priority for the US, unless the US plays host. East Asia is no more—there is only the Indopacific. There is the Quad and Aukus, loose military partnerships centered around containing China’s maritime ambitions. American worldview is pivoting to India and the INDOpacific being the center of Asia, and the red carpet is being rolled out to an immense population that can do no wrong. I fear the consequence of unbridled ascent. Note: the Americans no longer need China to buy its debt because they invented QE and explained it away using MMT.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: The manufacturer of China's large passenger airliner, C919, is receiving more orders. What does it mean for China's aerospace industry?
Answer: Comac has received over 1,500 orders for the 919. That is equal to 5 years of Chinese demand for narrow-bodies today. These figures are approximate, but the ballpark is revealing. The Chinese aviation market is huge, and Comac has a ready-made captive market, just because it is a national project in service of civilization pride. What Comac needs to do is build on the ARJ-21’s safety record, and iron out teething problems on the C919’s commercial rollout. Comac’s brand name must establish safe, reliable operation before competing on other metrics. Ramp-up will be cautious but we can expect delivery to pick up steadily from this year on. I won’t be surprised if one plane rolls out for delivery a day by 2030. The CJ-1000 engine variant should also make an appearance by 2030. There are also the C9x9 models in the works, along with superclusters of aviation suppliers centered around Comac’s production facilities. These will reintroduce efficiency and synergies that were dismantled through pork barrel politics and dominance of first world aviation tech decades ago. Exciting times as a new chapter in commercial aviation is written to democratize aviation tech. The true shocker will be the C9x9 widebodies. I’ve heard some interesting numbers wrt to price/specs. Gamechanging numbers.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Once Israel is required to pay reparations to the Palestinians for its genocide, will the USA pay for this like it does for Israel's healthcare, military, and other foreign "aid"? Americans cannot afford their own healthcare but pay for Israel's.
Answer: Reparations? We can’t even get Israel to stop the killing. It’s been 4 months of groundhog day, waking up to find today being a repeat of yesterday, as far as the Gaza strip is concerned. This is happening under the full glare of international media. Let’s cross the bridge when we get there. At this point, we are still floundering at sea, with no landfall in sight.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: Are you convinced by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's argument that the ringgit's decline does not reflect the reality of Malaysia's strengthening economy?
Answer: That’s a departure from Mahathir’s horror almost 30 years ago, when he complained loudly about the currency turmoil during the AFC that WIPED OUT TWO DECADES OF GROWTH IN TWO WEEKS, with Malaysia losing billions in purchasing power. The devaluation of the ringgit is structural and has been ongoing for 4 decades. In 1980, Singapore was still in a currency union with Malaysia. The SGD was 1:1 with the MYR. Today, it is >3.5, the lowest it has ever been. Is it a floor? I don’t think so. Malaysia is styling itself as a cheaper alternative to China in some sectors, and growth has mostly been padded by forex, particularly the reverse plaza accord over the past decade. Otherwise, the Malaysia today is not too different from the Malaysia of the 2000s, competitive advantage wise. Is Malaysia climbing out of covid? Certainly. But is it clawing back lost decades? I don’t see it. Put another way, can Malaysia grow in an appreciating ringgit environment? I welcome being proven wrong, but I’m not optimistic, given the feedback from the grapevine.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: How do you interpret Mike Gallagher's statement about US support for Taiwan being 'rock-solid' regardless of election outcomes?
Answer: It’s a soundbite. Ever since Richard the Watergate superstar paved the way for rapprochement with China in the 70s, American leaders have vacillated wildly in their public statements and action towards BOTH mainland and Taiwan. It must be remembered that Richard, and his sidekick Henry, kickstarted the complete betrayal of Taiwan and the KMT, at a time when Chiang Kai-Shek was still in charge. Richard gave the silent consent for the UN to expel Taiwan from the General Assembly, and replace the KMT’s China seat on the P5 with Beijing in 1971. Imagine, ceding de facto direct control of a P5 seat! Rapprochement culminated in the signing of the 3 Communiques with 3 separate American Administrations, both red and blue, setting out the terms of diplomacy between Washington and Beijing. America withdrew its troops from Taiwan, and broke off diplomatic recognition with Taiwan by 1980 (or thereabouts). Every first world nation followed suit. One of the last to normalize was militarily occupied South Korea in 1992. Today, 11 nations, representing 0.5% of the poorest and most disadvantaged among humanity, recognize Taipei in lieu of Beijing, and they are all to a fault economically tied to the American umbilical, especially aid. The question of Taiwan is being kept on life support by America, and fumes is all America can afford today. How has and indeed, how does America continue to view and treat Taiwan? The bulk of American public can’t even point to Taiwan on a map. American leaders painting a picture of “support” and “solidarity” for Taiwanese “democracy”, “liberty” and “rights” is nothing more than soundbite. If Generalissimo Chiang who helmed the P5 chair can be kicked asunder without being informed, whither Tsai and Lai today? Taiwan is merely a pawn on the chessboard. Let me repeat. Taiwan is merely a pawn on the chessboard. When it suits the hegemon, the piece is brought into play, a thorn in Beijing’s flesh. As long as it fulfills American objectives, the entire island can be sacrificed, every square inch of land, every man, woman and child. After all, it is “some island” far, far away. And mostly yellow to boot. That’s the callousness of American exceptionalism, even for “friends”. 美国爸爸靠不住。 Note: There is no genocide in Gaza, because there are still Palestinians alive. Hundreds of thousands Ukrainian bodies and >20 million refugees is a small price to pay for the Russian lives and coin they are taking to the grave. Not white enough equals cheap enough to be disposable.

Name: Bill Chen
Question: What do you think of U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken's theory of "If you're not at the table in the international system, you're going to be on the menu"?
Answer: That’s an insult, coming from the hegemon. Why? “At the table” describes a group of people who willingly come together to be ON THE LEVEL, and discuss the best way forward. America believes in its primacy and exceptionalism. The rules do not apply, and therefore, there is no being on the level when America’s on board. Case in point 1. America has just vetoed a Gaza ceasefire at the UN for the 4th time. That’s 4 months, >100 days of groundhog day violence and destruction, with more than 30,000 civilians already dead. No genocide, because there are still Palestinians alive. Besides, they are all Hamas vermin anyway. Case in point 2. America has ignored 30+ consecutive, near unanimous UN General Assembly resolutions passed over the last 30 YEARS to end the unfair embargo of Cuba. 30 YEARS. That’s Bill, George Jr., Barack, Donald and Joe, all giving the finger to the rest of humanity, including every member of the first world ex-America. Yes, even Canada and the UK. Case in point 3. America continues to “rent” Guantanamo from Cuba, a princely sum of $4,000 a year for an area greater than the size of Manhattan. The Cuban government has refused to recognize the validity of the perpetual lease signed in 1903 since the 50s, and has not accepted receipt of the “rent” for 7 decades, on real estate where war crimes, extraordinary rendition and torture has been conducted. And guess what? The United States formally recognizes the sovereignty of Cuba over Guantanamo! We don’t matter, and that’s why America is alone AT THE TABLE and the rest belong ON THE MENU. The Chinese say it best. 弱国无公义，弱国无外交。 Or, the friendly American diplomat’s age-old refrain for counterparts, “do you want to be consulted… or insulted?”

Question: How disastrous will things be for Intel and AMD in the Chinese market when China's Loongson chips catch up? Will they lodge a complaint to US congress about China not buying their stuff anymore?

Intel makes x86-based CPUs, and dabbles in iGPUs. x-86’s fate is chained to Microsoft’s Windows, although ARM is making inroads. Loongson or Longxin makes RISC-based CPUs, with independent IP that’s not licensed from third parties. This excludes Longxin from the Windows eco-system. It runs primarily on Linux, which is open-source. Which is fine, because the first world hasn’t developed great Chinese software options that are competitive with mainland ones. To add context, there are no Chinese IME (Input Method Editor) from the west that come close to being usable. Yes, Microsoft Pinyin/Swiftkeys/Gboard for Chinese input is lipstick on pigs next to mainland options. China will grow its own eco-system, adapting Linux as the native OS. Eventually, Longxin will have access to advanced nodes, and offer competitive chips at far lower prices across the performance spectrum. This will drive the adoption of Longxin-powered laptops/desktops, which is already turning up in offices today. This will reduce the market share of Windows/Mac, but they will still enjoy eco-system protection, unless geopolitics gets in the way. Check back in another 5 years, especially in the content creator realm. AI and fusion computing will drive huge changes.

Question: I noticed that Vietnamese and Japanese have many loanwords from Chinese, just like English did with Latin. So between them and English, which one is more influenced by the language they borrow from, such as structure, grammar, word order, etc.?
Answer: This is a random snippet of a Vietnamese news article. Modern Vietnamese script borrows from the latin alphabet, stacked heavily with diacritics for tones and phonemes. The content doesn’t matter. Pay attention to the structure of the words. Notice anything distinct from English? Yes, too many spaces. In other words, Vietnamese is mostly monosyllabic. Just like Chinese. Vietnamese is pinyin on steroids, and speaks to its deep Chinese roots. Vietnamese is not Chinese, but among the KJV or Chopsticks peoples, Vietnamese retains the most similarity, despite abandoning block writing. Where Vietnamese diverged from Chinese is its mapping of the syllable space to meaning. Mandarin kept it simple, by limiting the number of syllables to ~1,2000, including tones. This is because Chinese was designed from the ground up to be a written language, and many characters can share the same sound without ambiguity. But a spelled language like Vietnamese requires modification if it wanted to retain its monosyllabic character. That is why Vietnamese has over 17,000 possible syllables, with 6–7,000 in common use.

Question: Why does Singapore spend S$20.2b on defence for a small island with 6 million population? What is the rationale?
Answer: I have given various answers over the years examining this issue from several angles. I’ll use this opportunity to collect the illustrations I’ve used over the years here. First, a sense of scale. Singapore’s defense budget has been the largest item on the national budget since independence. We spend more on defense than education, or healthcare. We have maintained our spending way above Nato’s peacetime minimum of 2% GDP for more than 5 decades. For contrast, both Malaysia and Indonesia lowered their military spending below 1% post-AFC. Singapore prioritizes the military. In fact, Singapore is probably the most militarized piece of real estate in the world, in spending per unit area terms. How do we fund it? Through taxes. The last time I checked, our military consumed a sum equal to our entire commercial tax revenue. That is why any comparison with Hong Kong is flawed, because Hong Kong has had zero defense obligation in perpetuity. The fact that we remain competitive and deliver superior social outcomes in housing and education vis a vis the pearl of the orient speaks volumes about Singapore’s leadership. We have no right to be where we are, given the huge handicap that is in the ballpark of 500 billion SGD cumulatively, in current dollar terms. Imagine the social contract we could have offered diverting 0.5 trillion in tax revenue towards service provision, as well as the productivity boost freeing men from the burden of 24–30 months of conscription, in addition to reservist duty. Defense is a huge burden for Singapore. HUGE. Next, what is our stated aim for national defense? Our leaders have repeatedly admitted that Singapore is indefensible. And that is very clear from the map, because Singapore is a point target, with zero strategic depth. We are a strategic nightmare, surrounded on all sides by giant neighbors when we are not even self-sufficient in water, energy, or food. Let me repeat. Singapore is indefensible. But we are not defenseless. Ergo, the concept of Total Defense, preparing the citizenry to hunker down, take damage, and give as good as we get. All apartments have built in bomb shelters mandated by law, while our buildings and infrastructure are overbuilt specswise despite being free from natural disasters. For example, modern non-load bearing walls in HDB apartments are cast with gravel-mixed high-strength concrete, rather than bricks or cinder blocks. Why? Resist combat damage. All that extravagance, just to appear “not defenseless”? Yes. All that extravagance, just to appear “not defenseless”. Which brings us naturally to the rationale and calculus. The crux of Total Defense boils down to one word. Credibility. To make our neighbors understand we are no walkover, and it will be extremely costly pursuing war with Singapore. Yes, we will eventually lose, but the cost makes it unprofitable. Singapore is not defenseless. That is the wellspring of confidence Goh Chok Tong drew from when he advised us to brush off Mahathir’s “Singapore is a cat. There are many ways to skin it.” as a joke. Mahathir’s political acumen deemed it appropriate, and he repeated the line to receptive crowds all over Malaysia. Lee Hsien Loong as PM explained why we are not renewing the water agreement—every once in a while, some crazy politician will threaten to turn off the tap, to get us in line. We singlemindedly pursued water independence to nip unhappiness and resentment at the bud. Now, imagine if we had a third rate military. How would Mahathir’s “joke” be received? Would he have even cracked it, knowing provocative words from the sitting PM could have sounded like a clear warning of war? Would we have been afforded a full century to pursue the goal of water independence? If one is weak, even innocuous words delivered in the right tone can be interpreted as credible threat. “Business as usual” won’t be possible in such an environment. Singapore’s prosperity is founded on the credible ability to defend ourselves.

Question: Is Tucker Carlson competent enough to be a small town mayor in China?

One level up is Level 11, town-level HOD. Level 10 is Deputy Town Mayor. Level 9 is Town Mayor, responsible for an urban population > 2000, or rural population >20,000. Question: Why doesn’t CPC like to distribute handouts and instead spend money on infrastructure and other public services?
Answer: Many years ago, my boss asked, “kid, what’s the most expensive thing you see here?”, pointing out the window which overlooked the CBD. After thinking for a bit, I replied “probably UOB Plaza”. He gave a sly grin, but his answer has shaped my world-view since. “Kid, you’re too young. Always remember that the most expensive thing in any society is humans. Not infrastructure, not cars, not computers. Over the long term, it is the upkeep and training of humans that is the number one cost drain.” The problem with handouts is the cost to society. Productivity drops, labor force shrinks, taxes and public debt go up, while innovation goes downhill. This is not conjecture but data from the first world’s experiment with social security and healthcare. Immigration has papered over some of the cracks, but the problems brought about by fiscal holes have worsened continuously this century. Ultimately, what Chinese spend on infrastructure is a fraction of the long-term cost of handouts, as typically understood by first world citizens. However, it is not true that China does not distribute handouts, because it is an essential part of socialism and wealth transfer. The secret is in the manner of transfer. I’ll just describe 2 that came to mind. One. Stable prices through stockpiles. The Chinese government through SOEs have built the world’s largest stockpiles/reserves of many grains and commodities, such as rice, wheat, corn, iron/steel, rare earths and other essential raw materials. This is maintained at extravagant expense to prevent market disruption. As a result, the SOEs are often low-profit or even loss-making. This is a form of insurance and subsidy, so that daily essentials are affordable and more importantly, available to ordinary citizens. This is the primary reason why China has avoided the inflation wave that has rippled through most of the world economy post-covid. Two. Wealth transfer to the rural regions. Untold trillions have been sunk to upgrade connectivity to the villages and distribute land (or apartments in lieu) by household. Some projects don’t make economic sense but are pursued nonetheless to make a socialist stand. Lhasa, for example, is a Himalayan city of 500,000 at an elevation of 3,600m. Yet it is served by 3 railway lines and 4 highways, making it the best connected city at altitude in the history of man. Lhasa is the perfect advertisement to export the BRI model, especially in South America. What works in the Himalayas will work in the Andes. Handouts work. Just ask the hundreds of millions who have benefited in China. But it must be done cleverly, and sustainably, because human greed leads to laziness which collapses progress. I’ll leave the reader with some adverts from builders specializing in village houses… ahem… villas today. This particular company is from Hunan, historically a province that carried the stigma of being poor and backward. These are 4-storey, probably 400–500 sq. m built up, ample proof that poverty alleviation is working. Note: The first line on the bottom right reads “specialized in the design of build-to-order village houses”.

Question: Will Singaporean Chinese give their new generations children romanized names in Hokkien after Singapore officially promoting Mandarin and stigmatizing the dialect so many years, or just in Pinyin?
Answer: Legally, a Chinese Singaporean can have 3 names: chinese characters, pinyin, and dialect. There is no problem with the first two, because chinese characters are mapped one-to-one with pinyin, with the rare exception easily dealt with. For example, the protagonist 张无忌 is Zhang Wuji in pinyin, and that is the only way to write the name in the simplified script and pinyin, and one can consult a standard dictionary for verification. The problem is the dialect name. Unfortunately, there is no standardization possible with Singapore’s multi-dialect background, because each dialect has its own independent sound layer overlaid on the same set of characters. Besides, few dialects have pinyin-esque standardized romanization. For example, Hong Kong Cantonese uses the Standard, Yale, Lau, Lai, Cantonese pinyin, Guangdong and the more recent Jyutping systems. This results in a one-to-many mapping between the character name and the romanized dialect. Besides, many Hong Kongers retain idiosyncratic romanization that’s not part of any modern system. For example, the Cheung in Jacky Cheung Hok-Yau is obsolete Wade-Giles while his name in jyutping would be Jacky zoeng hok jau. Headturning weird isn’t it, for someone known unambiguously as 张学友? The problem is further complicated by the choice of dialect. There are 4 grandparents and the baby can inherit the heritage of 4 different dialects in practice. Personally, it was incredibly frustrating pursuing Cantonese romanization of my daughter’s name, because my own dialect name was a fusion Cantonese-Hokkien hybrid, to reflect my heritage. Besides, Cantonese names that sound nice/elegant have to be chosen IN CANTONESE, whereas Singaporeans usually choose the name in Mandarin, before deciding on the dialect romanization. Neither my wife’s nor my dialect name were spelled in standardized systems, and both of us were cantonese-hokkien. Eventually, we decided the little one will retain daddy’s non-standardized surname, and share the pinyin spelling for both the pinyin and dialect given name. There were two reasons driving the decision. One, her given name sounds elegant in Mandarin, but unwieldy in either Cantonese or Hokkien, especially spelled. Two, peace in the extended family is a marathon. My family’s struggle reflects why Singapore has retained an unique system of 3 legal names for the Chinese.

Question: Why does China permit the sale of iPhones by Apple in the Chinese market, while Chinese brands such as Huawei, Oppo, and Xiaomi face stringent restrictions in the US market?
Answer: Well, Japan put up walled gardens to grow their zaibatsu, today's keiretsu. Korea put up walled gardens to grow their chaebol. Taiwan put up walled gardens to grow practically the entire economy. All 3 were able to do so while enjoying open access to the US market, courtesy of the cold war and later, the rise of China. All 3 remain militarily dependent on the US. But look at Japan. It is no longer the tech leader in many industries. Toyota cannot compete in the ev segment today and even if it commits to a turnaround today, it will take years to catch up with byd's current production capacity. Sony is yesterday's Apple. Panasonic and Yuasa have been leapfrogged by Catl, longi and BYD. Mitsubishi, sumitimo, Olympus, Nissan and others have been hit by a wave of scandals. These are symptoms of atropy, the wasting away of muscle mass as competitive resistance ebbs. There is a similar effect observed in nature, and it is called the island rule, a phenomena where large mammals tend to shrink in size as isolated island populations, while small mammals tend to grow in size. This is what lack of competition in an artificially constrained environment does to living nature. We see the same signs appearing in Taiwan and Korea, several steps behind Japan. China didn’t pursue walled gardens the same way the Asian Tigers did. It is not about to undo almost 50 years of opening up by limiting competition, not when domestic options are within touching distance of industrial leaders in so many fields. The C919 is more than competent next to the A320/737. Li-Ning and Anta are a match for Adidas and Nike in design, materials and trendiness. BYD is outselling Tesla. And so on. The Chinese are globally competitive, just because whoever emerges from the cauldron that is the Chinese domestic market would have beaten global competition to get there. That’s the beauty of free markets, and open competition that reward winners on merit. Long may it continue.

The increase to 12-month conscription will help pad unit numbers in the combined armed forces, but Taiwan will have no choice but to continue downsizing in the coming decade, just because the replacement cohorts are way smaller than before. The Taiwan military is losing capability by the day, as institutional memory retire into the sunset and inadequately renewed. How many are willing to die for their half-baked beliefs? Not many. Taiwan has enough on its plate, and it is time to focus the top leadership on issues of livelihood, before crazy talk of war, war and war that has 0 chance of success. I wish Taiwan well.

Question: Why do the Chinese do long-term thinking and planning better, and why doesn't the rest of the world copy them?
Answer: I’d say the Japanese, Korean and others in the first world can make excellent plans too. For example, Europe led the world through the highly visible European Emission Standard for the past few decades, forcing the entire ICE industry to upgrade their engine tech to meet rising standards. That has improved the entire world’s air quality, particularly in urban areas. Unfortunately, capitalism stepped in and fraud was injected to game the system for profit. Enter diesel-gate, and because everyone was on the same playing field of marginal gains at the summit of ICE tech, people knew what was going on when fantastic numbers that passed environmental regulation were posted by company X. Company Y (and Z) had to emulate, or face market rejection. It’s money (or more accurately, profit) that spoils the broth, mostly, and the first world system of capitalism-driven economy is what ultimately derails the best-laid plans. For example, Europe (and the US) are in danger of derailing their EV ambitions due to inflation, on top of complicated geopolitics. The Chinese have extraordinary focus to deliver outcomes that can sometimes take generations. That’s akin to making deals with the grandpa for his grandson to deliver. Deng Xiaoping once said “let some people get rich first”, and we had the coastal SEZs boom, with local tax revenue retained to drive development. It was only decades later that taxes was redirected away, and a system of rich-poor city/region pairs established to shrink the wealth gap between those that “got rich first” and the rest in the queue. Deng’s promise made in the 20th century of prosperity for everyone will only be fulfilled in the 2040s/50s. Two full generations of sacrifice, and massive inequality, to build paradoxically, prosperous equality. Deng’s words are beyond reach of any non-mainland leader I know, and that list includes Lee Kuan Yew, but the Chinese nation embraced his hard-won (and very wise) words to heart. It’s the same story with China’s grain and commodity reserve, set up and maintained at extravagant cost to guarantee price stability, and continental scale projects such as the south-north water diversion, which is an ongoing decades-long project to redirect precious water resource. Another megaproject is high-speed rail, which has reached >45,000km in less than 20 years. Long horizon on capital recovery but affordable fares allow the Chinese to enjoy the world’s largest HSR network, already greater than the rest of the world combined. Evidently, there is more than capitalism at work, with profit not being the only or even the major consideration. It’s a different kind of thinking that drives the collective towards the goal of 天下太平 or peace under all-heaven.

Question: Why didn’t Boeing just design a new aircraft rather than “modernizing” the 737 by adding larger and more powerful engines to accommodate a bigger fuselage and more passengers?
Answer: Because of the type rating. For airliners, type ratings can make or break operations, because a single change to the aircraft type within the fleet can consume many months of human resources. Why? Every professional in the chain from crew (pilots and attendants) to maintenance engineers has to pass training programs and be type-certified, in order to work on the specific aircraft type. Note this is a legal requirement. No type rating, no work. A manufacturer will do all it can to introduce new models of the same type, to keep the type rating, and retain customers. That is why we have had multiple generations of the 737 over decades, as Boeing’s narrow-body representative in the airliner market.

Question: Do the Chinese know how much worse a war with the United States would be for their country than for the Americans?
Answer: The framing of the question betrays the deeply embedded values of a people who wage war for profit. China, as in the PRC, has never engaged in a war for profit in its entire history. China did not pursue land-grab or impose severe pre-conditions for the suing of peace. China merely wanted its voice heard when it said “no” to developments at its doorstep, and when all diplomatic avenues had been exhausted, demonstrated show-of-strength restraint to force the refusal through. There is no profit calculus when it comes to the upholding of territorial sovereignty. The Chinese are prepared to pay any cost—but not any more blood than necessary—to do so. Americans will not like the price of an unwinnable war with China, because the Chinese will not budge on issues of sovereignty. And any East Asian nation that seeks to reprise the Ukraine proxy role will find its economy devastated until relations are restored with the hub of Asia. Question: Does Hong Kong have a good government?
Answer: Insofar as a city government, it does the basics very well, namely tax collection and its EFFICIENT redistribution. Hong Kong has very good healthcare, and enjoys the world’s highest life expectancy, overtaking Japan in recent years. It also has pretty good social safety nets, by East Asian standards. Crime is low, while the civil service has low corruption, high trust and delivers consistent, high quality outcomes. All this from a tax base that’s one of the lowest in the world, all the more remarkable because Hong Kong has little to zero natural resource wealth to speak of. There is much to be proud of. However, its fraught history and Hong Kong’s status as a separate and distinct WTO member makes the world think of it as a city state, when the head honcho is merely a Chief Executive, rather than PM or President. By the standards of a city state, Hong Kong has failed in self-governance post-handover. Otherwise, the 2019 riots (which was a explosion in pent-up rage) would not have happened. In other words, the civil service is fine, but the elected leadership isn’t, because they have not had the baptism of fire street fighting through the political cauldron of domestic, regional and international politics. More simply, civil servants lack the aptitude for statecraft, mostly. For one, Hong Kong does not have to spend on defense, or foreign policy. It also does not have to contribute to Beijing’s coffers. Land-scarce Hong Kong can also tap the mainland for resources, such as energy and water. Hong Kong is set up to run like a city, and not a state. Unfortunately, the terms of handover tie Beijing’s hands, and it is unlikely Hong Kong will luck into a leadership that’s suitable for self-rule. I am quietly optimistic that having run itself aground, the Hong Kong ship has been refloated and is being towed back to the yard for retrofitting. As second gen diaspora, I wish Hong Kong well.

Question: It is estimated that China would lose its Navy, lose its critical infrastructure, be forced to renounce its claims to Taiwan, be blockaded and sanctioned and lose at least tens of thousands of troops in an attempt on Taiwan. How foolish is China?

What America is pouring into Indopacom is very far from adequate, let alone a credible threat to the projected outcome. Think again, harder, when it comes to China.

Question: What will happen to Singapore’s transport minister S Iswaran if he’s convicted of corruption?

Question: What's wrong with Malaysia? China completed 28,000 km of HSR. Malaysia still has not started to build 280 miles of KL-Sin HSR after 20 years of talking about it

Now, we have come back full circle. “This is a good project. We want back.” Will she? Won’t she? Can the project endure leadership transition? Are there any more skeletons in the closet? It is just a black hole of intrigue, as far as the future’s concerned. Indonesia has its first HSR line. Malaysia needs to play catchup.

Question: Do you believe that Beijing can manage China's property crisis without it spilling over to the rest of the economy?
Answer: Certainly. First, China has extraordinary control over the price of goods in the economy, Why? The Chinese government has the world’s best stocked larder and warehouses for food and commodities. These are strategic, nationwide stockpiles painstakingly built up over decades, with SOEs keeping a watchful eye on supply. This is why China barely hiccuped when the swine flu decimated pig farming, or when covid necessitated repeated lockdowns. In other words, there is incredible stability built into the Chinese economy. Two, the days of raising expensive capital to chase property appreciation is no more, even in the lower tiers. Domestic lending criteria has tightened significantly, especially for big developers, and Xu Jiayin is in jail awaiting trial, the poster boy for profligate, and ultimately ruinous ambition. Foreign capital is staying away after the fallout, and the sector as a whole is being shunned by capital. Three, China has plenty of infrastructure to build or improve on, with >200m chinese in the queue for urbanization. Coupled with service improvements, these will drive real, organic growth in property prices for the next two decades, hopefully, in more realistic step with rising income. We live in a world where real estate in some Indian cities is more expensive than tier one cities in China today, so there is room for prices to rise tomorrow. Four, China has plenty of policy space to maneuver, because it hasn’t had to resort to GFC (and beyond) levels of policy support over covid, unlike the first world. The popping of the property bubble can therefore be cushioned through selective targeting of other economic sectors, without resorting to massive stimulus or extreme monetary policy. Real estate speculation is a humongous market worth trillions. It will take years of careful management to bring under control. But there are effective cards China hasn’t dealt, such as instituting a property tax. Note: GDP is transactional. Real estate is asset wealth.
